comments.text:
**Decision log, part 2 of 5: Lua errors, M3-D15 to M3-D22 and M3-D44 (M3 plan, 2026-10-21).**

Each decision gives what was decided, why, the alternatives rejected, and which tasks carry it out. Decisions marked **departure** change what the vision bead body or a later vision comment says; G2 (`omad-m3-widget-errors-backups-7qmx.7.2`) records each one as a vision comment. The one marked **owner-visible** (M3-D30) changes a README promise, and plan approval approved it. Decisions are numbered by when they were made, not by topic, so the topic groups below interleave (M3-D43 and M3-D44 were added before the third review, M3-D45 to M3-D48 in the third review).

Section labels (`§x.y`) and plan keys (A1 … G3) are resolved by the milestone epic body ("How to read the M3 beads") and the key → id comment. Code references are as of `af10e34`.

### Lua errors

#### M3-D15: BugGrabber comes from WowAce's SVN through a new `wowace:` source
- **Decision.** A new keyless source fetches WowAce projects from their public SVN tags. It supports exactly the **source-ready subset** of WowAce packaging that BugGrabber needs, verified against its tree (§2.6), and refuses anything else.
  - **Ref forms:**
    - `wowace:<slug>` (the newest stable tag);
    - `wowace:<slug>#<tag>` (pinned tag);
    - `wowace:<slug>#r<rev>` (a trunk peg revision);
    - pasted links `https://repos.wowace.com/wow/<slug>/…` and `https://www.wowace.com/projects/<slug>`.
  - **Host.** `repos.wowace.com` joins the always-allowed list.
  - **Resolving a release.** One `PROPFIND` (`Depth: 1`) on `tags/` lists every tag with its `version-name`, the revision at which that tag directory last changed (§2.6). The newest stable tag is chosen from those names.
  - **Fetching a tree immutably.** Every directory listing and every file of tag `T` is fetched through `!svn/bc/<rev(T)>/tags/<T>/…`, the tag as of its last-changed revision. A tag that someone moves or edits mid-fetch therefore cannot produce a mixed-revision addon. A `#r<rev>` ref fetches `!svn/bc/<rev>/trunk/…`, which is pinned by construction.
  - **Identity.**
    - The display version is the tag name, because the TOC says `@project-version@`.
    - The release id is `wowace:<slug>@<tag>` (or `@r<rev>`). The resolved revision is recorded alongside it in the release, the lock entry and the blob-cache key (`wowace:<slug>/tags/<tag>@r<rev>`).
    - The release changes when the newest stable tag name changes, or when the same tag's `version-name` moves (a re-tag, shown as "v12.1.0 (re-tagged upstream)"). Commits elsewhere in the repository move neither, so they never show as phantom updates. That is why the repository's youngest revision is never used as identity.
    - `sync --locked` and a reinstall fetch the recorded revision, never the tag's current state.
  - **Packaging subset.** The zip is assembled, deterministically, as a packager would build this project, or the candidate is refused with reason `packaging_unsupported` in `no_compatible_release`'s `details.tried[]`:
    - `.pkgmeta` keys: `package-as` is honoured. It must pass `FolderName::new`, or the candidate is refused. Metadata-only keys are ignored: `manual-changelog`, `changelog-title`, `license-output`, `required-dependencies`, `optional-dependencies`, `tools-used`, `wowi-*`, and `enable-nolib-creation: no`. **Any other key** is refused: `externals`, `ignore`, `plain-copy`, `move-folders`, `enable-toc-creation: yes`, or one not listed.
    - Keywords: `@project-version@` in a `.toc` is replaced with the tag name, which is what the packager does. Any other `@word@` or `@word(…)@` token in a `.toc`, `.lua` or `.xml` file is refused, and so is any build-type block marker (`--@`, `<!--@`, `#@`).
    - Dotfiles are skipped, as the packager skips them.
  - Archive inspection and TOC verification then run unchanged.
- **Why.**
  - It is BugGrabber's upstream: the files are byte-identical to the GitHub mirror, and the tags are official.
  - It is keyless, and it serves both modern BugGrabber and r152, the last 3.3.5-era revision (GPL).
  - Without a source, `errors` would begin with "download this in a browser", which contradicts G2 (keyless by default) in the one feature that most needs a dependency.
  - **"No externals" alone would not make a source tree installable.** Packaging can move, ignore, substitute and comment out code. Shipping an unbuilt tree that happens to load would be a silent correctness bug. Supporting only what was verified, and refusing the rest by name, keeps the source honest.
- **Rejected** (evidence in §2.6):
  - (i) `hippuli/BugGrabber`: since v11.2.7 every build is bcc-only.
  - (ii) `curseforge-mirror/bug-grabber`: re-tagged several times a day (100 releases in three weeks, which would mean phantom updates), no `release.json`, REST needed to list assets, and a third party.
  - (iii) CurseForge's undocumented website API: terms risk, and contrary to D4.
  - (iv) `--file` only: a poor experience, kept as a fallback.
  - (v) Bundling BugGrabber in omaddons: modern BugGrabber is "All Rights Reserved".
  - (vi) Live tag paths with a sorted, timestamp-fixed zip (the first draft): deterministic serialization of a tree that may itself be mixed.
  - (vii) The repository's youngest revision as release identity: every unrelated commit would look like an update.
  - (viii) Advertising every no-externals project as supported.
- **Departure.** The handoff (vision comment 606) listed "a documented git mirror, CurseForge in M5, or a manual --file install". This is a fourth option, chosen with evidence. G2 records it, along with the new host (D13 allowlist).
- **Tasks:** C1, C2, C3.

#### M3-D16: same-name catalog variants select by disjoint client families
- **Decision.** Catalog entries may share a `name` (and aliases) when their `families` sets are **pairwise disjoint**. Each such entry is a **variant** with a stable identity, `<name>#<variant>`, where `variant` is a required key whenever a name has more than one entry (for example `BugGrabber#modern`, `BugGrabber#r152`).
  - **Validation** at catalog load, in the embedded catalog and after every `catalog.d` file: overlapping family sets for one name are an error. So are an alias claimed by two different names, and a variant key that is missing or repeated.
  - **Resolution.** A name resolves against the **target's actual family**: the variant whose `families` contains it.
    - No variant covers the family: the catalog has no entry for that target. `install` reports it as it reports any uncatalogued name, and `errors` says "no BugGrabber build for this client is known" (C3).
    - Without `-t`, resolution uses the default target's family. With no default target, `info` shows the variant covering `mainline`, else the first in family order, and lists the others' families.
    - TOC verification remains the final compatibility check for whatever is resolved.
  - **Merging `catalog.d`** works on identities, not bare names (`Catalog::apply` today upserts by name, §2.1):
    - an override naming `name` and `variant` replaces or removes only that variant;
    - an override naming only `name` replaces **all** variants of that name with itself, or removes them all with `remove = true`;
    - after merging, the disjointness rule is checked again, and a file that breaks it is skipped whole with `catalog_override_invalid`, as today.
  - Merge, `by_name`, `search`, `info`, `install` and dependency resolution all go through one `Catalog::resolve(name, family)` function.
  - **Shipped variants:**
    - `BugGrabber#modern`: `wowace:bug-grabber`, every modern family;
    - `BugGrabber#r152`: `wowace:bug-grabber#r152`, family `wrath-legacy`;
    - further legacy variants (for example `#r<rev>` for `tbc-legacy`, `cata-legacy` or `mists-legacy`), added only after C3's live probe verifies each one's TOC interface. Each gets its own disjoint family set.
- **Why.**
  - `omaddons install buggrabber -t wotlk` must just work.
  - The first draft allowed duplicates only across generations (modern vs `*-legacy`). The plan's own TBC, Cata and Mists legacy builds are all one generation, so its validator would have rejected them. Worse, today's merge collapses same-name entries before any validator runs (review finding, §2.1).
  - Disjoint family sets are the smallest rule that is both correct and checkable. They also guarantee that a vanilla-legacy client is never offered a build that only some other legacy family has.
- **Rejected:**
  - a distinct name (`BugGrabber-335`), which users would not guess;
  - generation as the selector (too coarse);
  - a general rule engine over interface numbers (speculative).
- **Tasks:** C3.

#### M3-D17: the SavedVariables parser
- **Decision.** `src/lua.rs` is the hand-written, infallible parser of the Lua-literal subset the client writes, plus some tolerance (B1's grammar, §9.1).
  - **Input.** `&[u8]`, capped by `SAVEDVARIABLES_MAX_BYTES` (64 MiB, reserved).
  - **Output.** `Parsed { globals: BTreeMap<String, Value>, issues: Vec<LuaIssue>, complete: bool }`, where `Value` is `Nil | Bool | Int(i64) | Num(f64) | Str(Vec<u8>) | Table(Table)` and `Table` is `{ array: Vec<Value>, hash: Vec<(Key, Value)> }`.
    - Strings stay bytes, because WoW strings are bytes. They become text only at render time.
    - Positional fields fill `array` in order; bracketed integer keys go to `hash` and are merged by the decoder.
  - **Skip mode.** Only the globals the caller asks for are built. Others are scanned without allocating.
  - **Limits.** Every bound holds in build and skip mode alike:
    - input bytes: `SAVEDVARIABLES_MAX_BYTES` (64 MiB, read with `read_bounded`);
    - nesting depth: `LUA_MAX_DEPTH = 64`, counted in skip mode too, where nothing is allocated;
    - nodes built: `LUA_MAX_NODES = 2,000,000`;
    - built payload: string bytes copied out of the input never exceed the input's length, by construction;
    - issues recorded: `LUA_MAX_ISSUES = 64`, after which only a `suppressed_issues` count grows.
  - **Linear progress.** The cursor never moves backwards. Every loop iteration either consumes at least one byte or pops the depth stack. Resynchronization scans forward from the error to the next top-level `Name =` and never rescans a suffix. A debug-build step counter asserts at most `4 × len + 2 × LUA_MAX_DEPTH` steps, and the fuzz target checks it. So total work is linear in the input, whatever it holds.
  - **Issues.** Truncation, a bad escape, depth or a node cap, an unexpected byte: each is recorded with a byte offset, up to the issue cap.
  - **Tests.** Proptests, a fuzz target `savedvariables`, seeds for both file formats, and adversarial resource tests. Those cover tiny-token tables, a huge long key, a flood of malformed fragments and deep skipped globals, with peak memory and time measured, not just "no crash".
- **Why.** The same design as the TOC and `product.db` readers (§2.1): untrusted input, never panic, bounded, fuzzed. The client's format is regular enough that a full Lua lexer is unnecessary, and the tolerance covers hand-edited files.
  - The widget refreshes `errors` automatically, so the parser's worst case is a shell-integration reliability property, not just a fuzzing concern. A file full of malformed fragments must not cost more memory in issue records than its own size, so issues are capped.
- **Rejected:**
  - (i) Embedding a Lua VM such as `mlua`: a C dependency, and it executes code.
  - (ii) A general Lua parser crate: no fit in the dependency policy, and overkill.
- **Tasks:** B1.

#### M3-D18: attributing an error to an addon
- **Decision.** These are B4's attribution rules (§9.3), in order:
  1. Protected-call events (`[ADDON_ACTION_BLOCKED|FORBIDDEN] … '<Folder>'`) go to the quoted folder.
  2. A `LUA_WARNING: ` prefix is stripped.
  3. Frames are taken from the message location, then from stack lines. r152 frames come from the message before `"\nLocals:|r\n"`.
  4. The folder is read from each frame's path. This covers all three stack eras, `...`-truncated paths (resolved by unique suffix match against installed folders), r152's `Folder-version` and `Major-Minor (Folder)` forms, and the trailing `-<n>` versions from BugGrabber ≤ v12.0.2.
  5. Each frame is classified:
     - Blizzard: `Blizzard_*`, or `Interface/FrameXML|SharedXML|GlueXML`;
     - self: `!BugGrabber`, `BugSack`;
     - library: any path segment `Libs|Lib|Libraries|Embeds|Externals`, `Lib[A-Z0-9]…`, `LibStub`, or `Name-N.N`;
     - otherwise addon.
  6. Attribution goes to the first addon frame. Failing that, the first library frame's folder; failing that, `blizzard` or `unknown`.
  7. The folder maps to the managed addon that owns it, through the target's records. DBM-Core and DBM-GUI both map to DBM.
  8. **Every attribution carries its evidence:**
     - `method`: `protected_call`, `first_addon_frame`, `library_frame`, `blizzard_only` or `none`;
     - `confidence`: `high` for a protected call naming an installed folder, or a first addon frame read from a full path; `medium` for a frame resolved from a `...`-truncated path by unique suffix, from r152's `Folder-version` form, or from a library frame; `low` for a message location only, or nothing.
- **Wording.** Output says "likely source", never "caused by". An available update is offered as "may fix it", never as a promised fix.
  - A taint error (`ADDON_ACTION_BLOCKED`) names the addon whose call was blocked, which is often a victim rather than the culprit. Its `method` is `protected_call` and the human text says "blocked call from".
  - WeakAuras custom code is attributed to WeakAuras with `medium` confidence, and the frame is labelled "custom code" (B4's attribution rules (§9.3)).
- **Why.** "First frame" or "first library frame" blames whichever addon's copy of CallbackHandler won LibStub's race (Questie issue 7959, §2.6). The first non-library addon frame is what a human reading the stack would pick.
  - It is still a heuristic. A stack shows where the error surfaced, not proof of the root cause. Showing the method and confidence lets humans and agents weigh it, and keeps the tool from overstating.
- **Rejected:** the message location only. It is truncated and often a library.
- **Tasks:** B4, B6.

#### M3-D19: what counts as a *new* error, and dismissal as durable user state
- **Decision.** "New" is decided per **database**: one BugGrabber file of one account, or one embedding provider's file (M3-D44). Received reports are never new (M3-D21).
  - **The baseline of a database** combines two sources:
    - the **acknowledged session** `acked_session`, with the time of the dismissal `acked_at`: a user decision kept in `<state>/errors_ack.json` (kind `errors_ack`, 1.0), written only by `errors dismiss`;
    - the **first-read baseline**, an observation kept in the errors memo (M3-D20). It is set when `errors` first reads a database with no memo entry: to `acked_session` when a valid acknowledgement exists, and otherwise to `DB session − 1`, so that only the latest UI session's errors count as new. Afterwards it never moves on its own: errors from every later session, including several `/reload`s within one evening, stay new until dismissed.

    The baseline is the larger of the two. Wiping `<cache>` therefore never hides an error the user did not dismiss: with an acknowledgement, the first-read baseline is rebuilt from it. With none, a wipe resets "new" to the latest session's errors, and README says so ("deleting the cache forgets which older errors were new").
  - **An entry is new** when it is local, its database's file is within the age limit, **and either** its `session` is greater than the baseline, **or** an acknowledgement exists and its session's newest time evidence proves that session occurred after `acked_at` (`TimeEvidence::at_or_after(acked_at) == Yes`, B3's decoding rules (§9.2)).
    - The time clause is decided **per (database, session)**, not per entry, so `errors` and `status --cached`, which keeps only per-session counts and newest times, always agree.
    - A session is one UI load. One that ended after the dismissal and carries a number at or below the acknowledged one can only come from a reset or replaced database, and all its entries postdate the dismissal.
  - **Reset and replacement.** An acknowledgement or a first-read baseline above the database's current `session` cannot belong to this database's history. That happens after `/bugsack reset` (session back to 1), a restored `WTF/` or a copied file, and that value is void while it is above the session.
    - **The first-read baseline is made sticky by its writer.** When `errors` (or `errors dismiss`) observes a database whose `session` is below the memo's first-read baseline, it rewrites that baseline to 0 in the memo, so everything since the reset is new. That stays true after the reset database passes the old number again. `status --cached`, which writes nothing, treats such a baseline as 0 for that call.
    - Voiding an acknowledgement by session alone is not sticky either: once a reset database passes the old number, a stale acknowledgement would apply again. The time clause above makes that harmless. Every error that occurred after the dismissal is new, whatever session number it carries, so a revived acknowledgement can only hide errors that predate the dismissal itself.
    - An integer time proves occurrence; a string time proves it only when it is after `acked_at`, since a first capture after the dismissal implies the error happened after it (B3's decoding rules (§9.2)).
  - **Age limit.** A database whose file mtime is older than `ERRORS_NEW_MAX_AGE` (7 days) **at the time of the read** has no new errors. `status --cached` recomputes this against the clock on every call, from the mtime it observes. It never trusts a `new` count frozen into the memo.
  - **r152** writes one entry per session and duplicate, so the same rules apply per entry.
- **`errors dismiss [-t T]…`** is a subcommand (path `errors dismiss`, group Look, `mutates: true`), because mutation is classified per path (§2.1).
  - It reads each selected target's databases afresh and acknowledges, per complete database, `acked_session = DB session`.
  - A database read incompletely (`errors_partial`) is not acknowledged. The result is `partial: true` and names it.
  - It takes the global lock briefly (recovering first, comment 723) and writes `errors_ack.json` through fsx, in an untracked `Writer::Mutating` session. `State` and `History` already admit that writer (`scope.rs:102-111`), so no scope changes. It appends a settings history line of the new kind `dismiss`, releases the lock and rings the doorbell.
  - `--dry-run` reports what it would acknowledge, with a `precondition`, and writes nothing.
  - With `--if-match <token>` (M3-D46), the token covers each database's file stamp and session as observed by the read the user saw. A database that changed since then refuses the whole dismissal with `plan_stale`. The `errors` read exposes that token per target as `dismiss.precondition`.
  - A dismissal cannot be undone (settings lines are not undoable). It only removes the "new" mark; the errors stay listed.
  - The acknowledgement stores no diagnostic text: per target key and database key (a SHA-256 of the file's relative path, not the path), `{acked_session, acked_at}`.
- **Why session watermarks, and not per-fingerprint ones.** The client writes SavedVariables only when a UI session ends (§2.6), and the next session starts with a higher number. So an error that occurs after a dismissal always lands in a session above the acknowledged one, even when it is "the same error again". Modern BugGrabber moves a recurring entry's `session` forward, and r152 adds a new entry. A per-session watermark is therefore exact for BugGrabber's write model, and needs no message-derived state. The one case where session numbers lie, a reset database, is covered by the time clause.
  - The real race is a dismissal acknowledging a session the user never saw, which the token closes.
  - Per-fingerprint occurrence watermarks (the review's proposal) would add state and identity rules to solve a case that cannot arise with this write model. They would also need their own continuity rules. If a future BugGrabber writes mid-session, the database's observed session would stop advancing per write, and C2's live schema probe is the tripwire.
- **Why durable.** A dismissal is the user's decision, and `<cache>` is documented as safe to delete. Deleting it must never make the bar urgent again about errors the user already dismissed.
- **Rejected:**
  - (i) Time windows: the semantics of `time` vary by version.
  - (ii) No dismissing: a permanent urgent state.
  - (iii) `errors --dismiss` as a flag on a read command: it would make `app::mutates("errors")` false for a write.
  - (iv) Storing the dismissal in the cache memo (the first draft).
- **Tasks:** B6 (first-read baseline and new rule), B8 (dismiss, acknowledgement state), B7 (status).

#### M3-D20: the errors memo is derived; `status` stays write-free
- **Decision.** `<cache>/errors.json` (kind `errors_memo`, 1.0) is written by `errors` (the read) and by `errors dismiss` (B8), only from a **complete canonical observation** (B6), never from a filtered or truncated view, and only when its content changed.
  - **Per target key and per database it stores:**
    - the file's path relative to the client dir (local only), its `FileStamp` and the `SavedVariables/` dir's listing fingerprint;
    - the DB `session` and the first-read baseline (M3-D19);
    - counts of local entries per session: `{session: {entries, occurrences, newest_time}}`, where `newest_time` is that session's newest time evidence. `new` can then be recomputed against the baseline, the acknowledgement's `acked_at` and the clock without the file. Plus `received` (count only);
    - per-addon counts (`addon`, `folder`, `count`, `new`, `last_seen` with its time meaning);
    - the read outcome: `complete`, `partial` (with its reason) or `over_budget`. An over-budget file is recorded with its stamp, so the unchanged file is reported as incomplete rather than re-read on every doorbell;
    - the target's `capture` (`buggrabber`, `none`) and its probe coverage (accounts and files examined against the bounds, M3-D44).
  - **It stores no message, stack or locals text.** Deleting it deletes observations only. The acknowledgement lives in `<state>` (M3-D19).
  - **Readers:**
    - `status --cached` reads the memo and the acknowledgement, lstats the recorded files, and lists up to `ERRORS_MAX_ACCOUNTS` accounts' `SavedVariables/` dirs to spot new files.
      - A mismatch reports `state: "stale"`, with the last counts. A target with no memo entry reports `state: "unchecked"`.
      - `new` is recomputed from the per-session counts and newest times, the acknowledgement (and its time clause) and the file ages at the time of the call.
      - A recorded `partial` or `over_budget` outcome reports `state: "partial"` with the counts read. That is never a clean zero.
      - Coverage beyond the bounds is reported as `coverage: "truncated"`.
    - `status` (not cached) parses live (bounded, typically under 10 ms) and writes nothing.
    - The widget, on `stale` or `unchecked`, runs `errors` once, which rings the doorbell. It does not rerun on `partial`.
- **Why.**
  - `tests/status.rs:154-163` asserts `status` never writes, and M2-D15 made drift live and unpersisted for the same reason.
  - The memo is the M2 release-memo pattern (§2.2): derived, best effort, never fails a command.
  - Keeping message text out of it means no personal data is duplicated at rest.
  - Writing it only from the complete observation means `errors --addon DBM --limit 1` can never shrink what the bar knows (review finding).
- **Rejected:**
  - (i) `status --cached` parsing on every call: 2–20 ms per file breaks the 5 ms budget.
  - (ii) Letting `status` write the memo: it breaks the read-only invariant.
- **Tasks:** B6, B7.

#### M3-D21: privacy is a contract, enforced on every channel
- **Decision.** Privacy is defined by **what kind of text** may leave the process, not by which patterns get redacted. Pattern redaction cannot recognize a name an addon wrote into an error string (§2.6).
  - **Strict output, the default and `-v`.** It holds only code-derived and structured data:
    - the addon, its folders, `kind`, and `attribution` with its method and confidence (M3-D18);
    - the **location**: AddOns-relative path and line, from the message or the first frame;
    - the **message**, only when it matches a recognized template, else `null`. The templates are Lua 5.1's runtime messages (`attempt to index|call|compare|concatenate|perform arithmetic on …`, `bad argument #N to '…' (…)`, `stack overflow`, and their kin), Blizzard's protected-call messages (`[ADDON_ACTION_BLOCKED|FORBIDDEN] AddOn '…' tried to call the protected function '…'`) and a short list of known `LUA_WARNING` forms. Every quoted variable part must be a code identifier (`^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.:]*$` or `?`), or the template does not match. `message_kind` is `lua_runtime`, `blizzard` or `custom`. For `custom`, only `message_chars`, its length, is shown;
    - **stack frames:** each frame's path, line and function name (`in function 'X'`, `in function <file:line>`, `in main chunk`). Chunk frames (`[string "…"]`) show as `[custom code]`, never their contents. `[C]` and tail-call lines are folded. That is at most `ERRORS_STACK_LINES` = 6 frames by default, and 40 with `-v`;
    - counts, sessions, the time evidence (M3-D19, B3's decoding rules (§9.2)) and an opaque `fingerprint` (`e:` plus 16 hex digits of a SHA-256 over the normalized message and location);
    - accounts labelled `account 1…n`, in a stable order by folder name, which is never printed.

    `-v` adds only safe metadata: the full frame list, the per-database breakdown, and file paths with the account replaced by `account N`.
  - **`--raw-details`** (a new flag on `errors`) adds, per error, a `raw` block. It is best effort: it names the danger and promises no anonymity.
    - It holds the message's first line (at most `ERRORS_MESSAGE_MAX_CHARS` = 300), the raw frames (at most 40) with chunk contents cut to `ERRORS_CHUNK_MAX_CHARS` = 40, and `locals` (at most `ERRORS_LOCALS_MAX_CHARS` = 4,096).
    - It is sanitized: WoW UI escape codes are stripped (`toc::plain_title`'s rules); player GUIDs (`Player-\d+-[0-9A-F]{8}`) and player links (`|Hplayer:…|h…|h`) become `<player>`; control characters other than `\n` are dropped; and every account, realm and character folder name found under this client's `WTF/Account/` becomes `<account>`, `<realm>` or `<character>`.
    - The human output adds the line "raw details may contain other players' names and your own code; share with care". The JSON carries `raw_details: true` in `data`.
  - **Received reports** (a `source` key, §2.6) carry `origin: "received"`, and the sender's name is never kept. They are excluded from new counts, `--check`, notifications, `commands[]` recommendations and `status`. Without `--received` they appear only as a per-target `received` count. `--received` lists them, marked, in their own groups.
  - **Every other channel follows the same rule.** One `privacy::WtfPathRedactor`, built from the client's `WTF/Account/` listing, maps account, realm and character components to `account N`, `realm N` and `character N`. It is used:
    - in every progress message: backup and restore progress carries counts and a fixed label (`"WTF/ files"`), never a path;
    - in error `details` and warning texts that name a WTF path (`CloneError::Changed`, sanitized paths from `sv_skip`, import refusals);
    - in import validation, where archive paths get their own redactor from the archive's listing.

    Notifications carry names and counts only (M3-D14).
  - **At rest.** `<meta>/backups/` and every backup dir are created `0700`. Backups necessarily hold private data. Their summaries (`backup.json` fields shown by `backup list`) never do. Manifests are local-only.
- **Why.**
  - Vision §4.4 and vision §5.8 promise that personal data never appears by default. GUID and link redaction alone cannot keep that promise for arbitrary strings, and tests against three fixture names cannot prove anonymization (review finding).
  - A contract on *kinds of text* can be enforced and tested. Lua's runtime messages carry the diagnostic value humans and agents need, and they are code-derived. Custom messages are one explicit flag away.
  - Paths are personal too. The first draft streamed raw WTF paths in progress events, which the widget displays, and that is fixed here.
- **Rejected:**
  - (i) Showing the first line of every message by default with pattern redaction (the first draft): it cannot recognize names.
  - (ii) Hiding all message text, templates included: it loses most of the diagnostic value for no privacy gain.
  - (iii) Making `-v` the switch for free text: an ordinary verbosity flag should not quietly become a personal-data export.
- **Tasks:** A5 (the shared `WtfPathRedactor` and the `assert_private` helpers; added in the third review, so it owns what earlier drafts gave to B5 and D1), B5 (sanitizer, templates, the strict renderer), B6 (flags and channels), D1 (progress with counts and fixed labels), D10 (import messages), F8 (notifications).

#### M3-D22: `errors` exit codes
- **Decision.** `errors` exits 0 whether or not errors exist. Errors are status, not failure. A target without BugGrabber is listed with `capture: "none"` and an install hint in `commands`; that is not an error.
  - **`--check`** exits 6 (`check_failed`, `data` kept), judged on the documented selection before display truncation. It fails when, for any selected target (`-t`, then `--addon`):
    - it has new local errors. With `--since`, an entry whose time cannot prove it is older than the cutoff (`uncertain`, B3's decoding rules (§9.2)) counts as matching, because a check must not pass by dropping an error that may be recent;
    - or its observation is incomplete (`partial`, `unreadable`, or bounds exhausted), which gives `details.reason: "incomplete"`. A check cannot certify what it could not read.
  - `--limit` never changes `--check`'s answer.
- **Why.** It matches `outdated --check` and the general exit dictionary (D18).
- **Tasks:** B6.

#### M3-D44: where `BugGrabberDB` is looked for, within bounds
- **Decision.** For each account of a target, `errors` reads `SavedVariables/!BugGrabber.lua` when the `!BugGrabber` folder is present, or when the file exists without it.
  - It also reads `SavedVariables/<Folder>.lua` for every other folder whose loaded TOC lists `BugGrabberDB` under `## SavedVariables`. Examples are bdUI, and copies embedded in Decursive and AdiBags.
  - Only the `BugGrabberDB` global is built (skip mode, M3-D17).
  - Directory and file names match ignoring case, and `sv_skip`'s rules apply: a symlink out of the client dir or a folder spelled two ways is skipped and counted.
  - **Bounds per target and per invocation**, each reported as truncated coverage when hit, never silently:
    - at most `ERRORS_MAX_ACCOUNTS` (32) account dirs examined;
    - at most `ERRORS_MAX_FILES` (64) candidate files parsed;
    - at most `ERRORS_MAX_TOTAL_BYTES` (256 MiB) read in one invocation across every target.
- **Why.** Some packs embed BugGrabber. The TOC parser already reports SavedVariables names, so the lookup is exact rather than a scan of every file. The bounds keep a strange tree (thousands of accounts from a sync tool) from turning a doorbell refresh into a long walk.
- **Tasks:** B5, B6.

comments.text:
**Decision log, part 3 of 5: backups and restore, M3-D23 to M3-D29 (M3 plan, 2026-10-21).**

Each decision gives what was decided, why, the alternatives rejected, and which tasks carry it out. Decisions marked **departure** change what the vision bead body or a later vision comment says; G2 (`omad-m3-widget-errors-backups-7qmx.7.2`) records each one as a vision comment. The one marked **owner-visible** (M3-D30) changes a README promise, and plan approval approved it. Decisions are numbered by when they were made, not by topic, so the topic groups below interleave (M3-D43 and M3-D44 were added before the third review, M3-D45 to M3-D48 in the third review).

Section labels (`§x.y`) and plan keys (A1 … G3) are resolved by the milestone epic body ("How to read the M3 beads") and the key → id comment. Code references are as of `af10e34`.

### Backups and restore

#### M3-D23: what a backup is
- **Decision.**
  - **Location.** `<meta>/backups/<id>/` (the `backups/` dir and every `<id>/` created `0700`) holds:
    - `backup.json` (kind `backup`, 1.0):
      - identity: `id`, `target` (key), `target_id`, `family`;
      - times: `created_at` (when this backup was published here) and `captured_at` (when its content was captured; for an import, the source's capture time);
      - `kind`, plus `trigger` (`pre_change|post_session`, automatic backups only), `actor`, `reason`;
      - `client_version`, `client_running`;
      - the counts `files`, `dirs`, `symlinks` and `skipped`, `bytes` (apparent), `reflinked` (`all|some|none`), `unsettled`;
      - `consistency` (`stable|best_effort`, below);
      - `integrity` (`metadata_only|verified|damaged`) with `verified_at` and `baseline` (`capture|import|later`, M3-D47);
      - `tool_version`, `source` (for imports) and `partial` (recovered backups only);
    - `manifest.json` (kind `backup_manifest`, 1.0): `[{path, kind, size, mode, mtime_ns, link?, sha256?}]`, relative to `WTF/`, as spelled on disk. `mode` is the **exact source mode** and `link` a symlink's target. `sha256` is present only when content was hashed at capture (`--verify`), at import, or by `backup verify`. It is local only, because it contains account names;
    - `addons.json` (kind `backup_addons`, 1.0), the **addon provenance**: for each managed addon of the target record at capture, `{name, folders[], version, source: {kind, ref, release_id}}`. It is copied from the record, and no SavedVariables is parsed. Addon names are not personal data, so `backup list -v` may show them;
    - `WTF/`: the tree.
  - **Kinds:** `manual`, `auto`, `before_restore`, `imported`, `recovered` (made by recovery from a rolled-back restore whose displaced data differed from any surviving copy, M3-D24 (c); `partial: true` when it holds only some files, and then it restores only with `--addon`).
  - **Ids** are ULIDs. A prefix of 8 or more characters selects one, as undo's prefixes do.
  - **How it is built:**
    1. Copy into `<meta>/stage/<tx>/backup/` in an **untracked** `Writer::Backup` session: `CloneFile` per file with deferred durability and the caller's `ClonePolicy` (M3-D30), `CreateDir` per dir, and `SymlinkAtomic` per symlink (never followed). Other file types are skipped and counted. No file is hashed unless `--verify`.
    2. **Directory modes.** Directories are created owner-writable, and stay so in the stored tree (`recorded mode | 0o700`), exactly as `keep_dir_mode` keeps staged trees prunable (§2.4 item 12). The exact mode is in the manifest. A restore applies the recorded modes to the staged tree, children first, before the exchange, so the restored `WTF/` matches the source exactly, a `0500` directory included.
    3. Run one `syncfs`.
    4. `RENAME_NOREPLACE` into `backups/<id>`.
  - **Capture consistency.** A tree is not captured atomically: FICLONE is atomic per file only (§2.4 item 8).
    - Each file's `FileStamp` is read before and after its copy. A mismatch is re-copied once; if it still differs, it counts as `unsettled`.
    - The root `WTF` directory's identity (device, inode, birth time) is read before and after the capture. A changed root means the tree was replaced (a concurrent restore, a sync tool), and the capture fails and is retried once.
    - After the copy, a second stat walk of the source is compared with the manifest: entry set, kinds, sizes and mtimes. That catches a file added, removed or changed after its own copy.
    - If either check differs, the whole capture is retried once (`BACKUP_CAPTURE_ATTEMPTS` = 2). If it still differs, the backup is published with `consistency: best_effort` and the warning `backup_unsettled`, with counts of changed, added and removed entries. An automatic backup that ends `best_effort` does not count as a checkpoint (M3-D31).
    - `stable` means **observed quiescent during capture**, not a filesystem snapshot, and the docs say so.
- **Why.**
  - Under `<meta>`, the backup is on the same filesystem as `WTF/`, so reflinks work and the restore exchange is atomic (D7).
  - The untracked staging session is the only fsx path that allows deferred durability (§2.4 item 6), and skipping hashing keeps a 500 MB copy under 1 s.
  - Stamps and the inventory recheck give honest evidence of what was captured, at the cost of two lstats per file. `consistency` and `integrity` keep the label from claiming more than that evidence shows (review finding: the first draft's `restorable: true` meant only "paths, kinds and sizes match").
  - The addon record costs a few hundred bytes. It lets a partial restore find an addon's files after the addon was removed or renamed a folder, and it tells the user which addon version wrote the settings (M3-D27).
- **Rejected:**
  - (i) Per-file SHA-256 at every create: about 0.5–1 s per 500 MB, which breaks the budget. It is opt-in (`--verify`, M3-D47).
  - (ii) A tar inside the client dir: no reflinks, slow.
  - (iii) Timestamp ids: collisions, and inconsistent with transaction ids.
  - (iv) Storing exact `0500` directory modes in the backup tree: a backup with an unwritable directory could not be pruned.
- **Tasks:** D1, D2.

#### M3-D24: a whole restore is one journaled exchange of the `WTF` directory
- **Decision.** `backup restore <id>` (without `--addon`) is an engine transaction of kind `restore` (`src/engine/restore.rs`):
  1. **Plan** (no lock), in this order (D8 owns it):
     - resolve the backup and take a **reader reservation** on it (M3-D48);
     - check that it is restorable and structurally complete;
     - check running (fail closed);
     - allocate the `TxId` and its `InflightLock`, so everything written from here on belongs to a transaction that retention can recognize.
  2. **Topology preflight** (no lock, before any copying). A whole restore needs a rename-compatible location, which a device comparison cannot prove (§2.4 item 16). `statx` with `STATX_MNT_ID` must show:
     - `<client dir>/WTF` is not a mount point (its mount id equals the client dir's);
     - `<meta>/stage/` is on the client dir's mount;
     - `WTF` is not a symlink out of the client dir (`scope_denied`, as before);
     - **the filesystem supports `RENAME_EXCHANGE`**: a probe exchanges two empty files in `<meta>/stage/<tx>/probe/` (on the client's mount, so on the same filesystem) and removes them. A crash leaves it inside the transaction's own stage dir, which the orphan sweep reclaims (`retention.rs:309-316` parses the `TxId`). A `--dry-run` writes nothing: it runs the `statx` checks only and reports `exchange: "unverified"`.

     Any failure refuses with the new error `filesystem_unsupported` (exit 4, not retryable): `details.reason` is `wtf_is_mount_point`, `stage_cross_mount` or `no_rename_exchange`. There is no argv alternative, because a partial restore needs the same capabilities. The prose fix reads "a restore needs WTF/ to be a plain directory on the same mount as Interface/, on a filesystem with atomic exchange (btrfs, ext4, xfs, tmpfs); otherwise copy what you need from the backup folder by hand with the game closed", and `details.backup_dir` names that folder. Nothing has been copied yet.
  3. **Precondition and the `before_restore` backup.** With `--if-match`, the token is compared now, before anything is copied (M3-D46). Then the `before_restore` backup is made (M3-D26), so a refusal above never costs a copy.
  4. **Stage** (no lock): reflink-copy `backups/<id>/WTF/` into `<meta>/stage/<tx>/WTF/` with an untracked tree clone that **does not hash**, apply the manifest's exact modes (M3-D23), then one `syncfs`.
     - Check the staged entry count and sizes against the backup's manifest, and fail (nothing changed) if the source vanished or changed mid-copy.
     - When the manifest has hashes (an imported or verified backup, M3-D47), hash the staged files and compare. A mismatch fails with `hash_mismatch` ("backup … is damaged"), nothing changed.
     - Take the stamp digests (M3-D25).
  5. **Lock and revalidate:** run recovery, registration, the generation check against the plan's generation (which, with `--if-match`, is the token's), the mount ids again, and a **fresh running check**, the last one before the live transition. The token itself is not recomputed under the lock: its file observations were taken before staging, and recomputing them would cost the lock-hold budget.
  6. **Journal** `prepared`: kind `restore`, `client_dir`, the new optional flag `writes_wtf: true`, `staged_stamp`, and `source_backup` (`{id, dir identity}`, so recovery can tell whether the source still exists). When there is no live `WTF/`, step 1 is a `Noreplace` and rollback moves it back. `creates_dirs` is not used, because it means "dirs recovery leaves" (`journal.rs:89-94`). Steps:
     - Exchange `stage/<tx>/WTF` ⇄ `<client dir>/WTF` (`Noreplace` when absent), purpose `SwapIn`;
     - Noreplace the old tree (now at the stage path) → `<meta>/snapshots/<tx>/WTF.previous`, purpose `OldToSnapshot`.
     - **No two-rename fallback.** If the exchange returns "unsupported", the step has not run: the transaction rolls back trivially and fails with `filesystem_unsupported` (`no_rename_exchange`). Nothing has moved.
  7. **Undo data first.** Before step 1, still under the lock: `snapshot_state` and the client snapshot dir `<meta>/snapshots/<tx>/`, as `tx.rs:908-910` orders it for AddOns.
  8. **Commit:** `swapped`; the record with `generation + 1`; the history line with the op `{"op":"wtf","folder":"WTF","addon":"","backup":"<id>","from":"backup","files":N}`; `committed`.
  9. **After commit:** ring the doorbell, release the reader reservation, clean up, run retention.

  **Required engine changes:**
  - **(a) Scopes.**
    - `Writer::BackupRestore` may rename `<client dir>/WTF` itself; the `Wtf` root accepts `Rename` from `BackupRestore` only. This is a scope-table change, recorded on the vision.
    - `history.jsonl` is already writable by `BackupRestore` through the `State` row (`scope.rs:102-106`). D5's scope test pins that, and adds `BackupRestore` to the `History` row only if the test shows the narrower row decides.
  - **(b) Recovery's writer follows the journal's content, not its kind.** A journal whose `prepared` line has `writes_wtf: true` recovers as `Writer::BackupRestore`; everything else stays `Mutating`.
    - Restores, undos of restores and partial restores all set the flag.
    - An undo-of-restore journal has kind `undo` (`undo.rs:322`), so selecting by kind would strand it.
  - **(c) Recovery keeps the engine's direction and adds three rules for `writes_wtf` journals.** The direction follows the **durable journal phase**: backward before `swapped`, forward from it. The rename having executed does not, by itself, select roll-forward.
    1. **Wait while the game runs.** A `writes_wtf` journal with any step recorded is not touched while its client runs, while running is unknown, or while its target is not discovered (an unmounted disk), because rolling back renames under `WTF/`.
       - Recovery leaves it, warns `journal_pending` ("… waits for the game to exit"), and lets other targets' recovery proceed (comment 667). A journal with no step recorded moves nothing, so it recovers at once: it applies rule 3's source check to its stage (a staged copy whose source backup is gone is preserved), then prunes the stage.
       - **In-process recovery** (`recover_tx`, right after a failure in the commit window) makes the same fresh running check rather than assume that the check a few milliseconds earlier still holds. A client that started in between leaves the journal pending.
       - Process detection is a refusal check, not an exclusion lock. The game does not take omaddons' lock, so it can launch between the final check and the exchange. Then it reads one consistent tree (the exchange is atomic) and may write its in-memory settings over the restored files at logout. The undo snapshot still holds the pre-restore tree. This residual race is documented in README's Safety model, and no cooperating launcher guard exists.
    2. **Unexpected identities are ambiguous, never attributed.** A rollback step whose paths match neither their before nor their after identity (`ran()`'s error case, `journal.rs:959-964`) proves only that the recorded transition is no longer recognizable. It does not prove who changed it: the game, a sync tool, a manual move or an earlier interrupted recovery. The live path is **never** touched by such a step.
       - **Recognized:** the step's displaced side is found at its recorded path with its recorded identity. The displaced side is the step's non-live path only: for an exchange, the entry at the stage or snapshot path that rollback would move back into `WTF`; for a `Noreplace` out of the live path (live → stage or snapshot), its destination.
       - **A `Noreplace` into the live path has no displaced side.** These are the steps that restore a file absent before, and a whole restore onto a client with no `WTF/`. If its source path is empty and the live entry is not the one recorded, the game or a tool replaced our restored entry: nothing of ours sits outside `WTF/` any more. Recovery leaves the live path as it is and continues. The replaced entry was a copy of the backup, whose survival rule 3's source check covers. For example, the old tree sits at `WTF.previous` while something new occupies the live `WTF`. That displaced version is preserved (rule 3), and rollback continues with the next step.
       - **Unrecognized:** neither side can be found where and as recorded. Recovery stops before any cleanup. The journal, the stage and the snapshots stay as they are, with `journal_pending` and `details.reason: "unexpected_state"`, which is M2's manual-repair state. Every later change on that client fails until it is resolved, and the M4 doctor automates that. Other clients are unaffected.
    3. **Displaced versions get a durable home before anything is pruned, through a journaled, resumable intent.**
       - **A journal that already holds a `preserve` line has finished its reverse walk.** Recovery skips `roll_back` and candidate collection, which would otherwise find every step in neither state because the items have moved, and resumes at the first unfinished protocol step below, locating each item at its `path` or at its assembly destination.
       - Otherwise, after the reverse walk, recovery collects the preservation candidates:
         - each recognized displaced version from rule 2;
         - the tree or files at `stage/<tx>/WTF` whose stamps differ from `staged_stamp` (whole) or `staged_files` (partial);
         - a staged copy whose stamps are unchanged but whose source backup no longer exists with its recorded identity (pruned meanwhile). Then the stage holds the last copy of that content, and a metadata match proves nothing about a surviving copy.

       With no candidates, cleanup runs as today. Otherwise:
       1. **Intent.** Reserve a backup id once and append a `preserve` journal line: `{id, items: [{path, identity, rel}], assembly: <meta>/stage/<tx>/recovered/<id>/}`. It is fsynced before anything moves. A resumed recovery reuses this line and id, and never generates a second one.
       2. **Move** each item into the assembly dir (`WTF/` for a tree, `WTF/<rel>` for files). Before each move, recovery checks the item's identity at its source and at its destination, so a repeat is idempotent.
       3. **Describe:** write `manifest.json` (a stat walk) and `backup.json` (kind `recovered`, `partial` when not a whole tree, `captured_at` = now, `consistency: best_effort`) into the assembly, then `syncfs`.
       4. **Publish:** `Noreplace` the assembly → `backups/<id>`. A listing never sees a half-made backup. If `backups/<id>` already holds the same identity, this step is already done.
       5. **Complete:** append `preserved {id}`. Only after every `preserve` line has its `preserved` line do the stage, snapshot and journal cleanups run. Then warn `restore_rolled_back` with fix `omaddons backup restore <id> -t <target>` (with `--addon` for a partial one).

       **Any I/O error, disk-full or identity surprise during these steps** stops recovery with everything in place: `journal_pending`, `details.reason: "preservation_incomplete"`. The next recovery resumes from the journal. Recovery never deletes something to make progress.
    - **Why rollback, not roll-forward.** The first draft rolled restores forward. Review showed it would need the planned steps recorded in `Prepared`, recovery journaling its own steps, and changes to the dead-snapshot sweep, which would otherwise delete a rolled-forward restore's snapshots (`journal.rs:781-797`). Rollback plus these rules keeps one direction in the engine and still never silently discards a play session (vision D33).
    - **Why an intent record.** Without one, a crash after moving a displaced tree but before writing its `backup.json` leaves the next recovery unable to recognize the half-made backup. It would generate a new id, or list the tree as damaged. The preservation step is itself a transition, so it gets the same write-ahead discipline as everything else (review finding).
    - The restore command itself refuses with `game_running` before staging.
  - **(d) Retention guards.** A snapshot dir holding `WTF.previous` counts as holding the only copy (the orphan sweep never deletes it), and `most_recent` ignores `backup` history lines. A stage dir whose journal holds a `preserve` line without its `preserved` line is never pruned: its journal exists, and the orphan rule is `dead = !is_live && !journal.exists()` (§2.4 item 15).
  - **(e) New engine failpoints:**
    - `engine.restore.staged`, `engine.restore.exchanged`, `engine.restore.snapshotted` (D5);
    - `engine.preserve.intent`, `engine.preserve.moved`, `engine.preserve.published` (D14).
  - **(f) Fail-closed reading** of the journals these changes write (M3-D45).
- **Why.**
  - `RENAME_EXCHANGE` of a directory is atomic, so `WTF/` is wholly old or wholly new at every instant. That is the engine's invariant, extended from AddOns folders to `WTF/`. Refusing where exchange is impossible keeps the promise literal. A silent two-rename fallback would leave a moment with no `WTF/`, and a game launched then would write a fresh default one.
  - The existing journal, recovery and identity checks work unchanged for a directory step (§2.4 item 1). The changes are exactly the blockers §2.4 found (items 2, 3 and 5), plus the preservation protocol the third review showed was missing.
- **Rejected:**
  - (i) Restoring file by file: thousands of steps and a long lock.
  - (ii) Copying over the live `WTF/`: not atomic.
  - (iii) A restore outside the engine: a second recovery path, which D26 forbids.
  - (iv) The two-rename fallback for a whole restore (the first draft): invisible weakening of the advertised invariant.
  - (v) "The game's writes win", inferring the author of a change from an inode mismatch (the first draft).
  - (vi) A fresh backup id per recovery attempt (the first draft): it cannot be resumed.
  - (vii) An explicit `--allow-gap` mode for filesystems without exchange: one more flag and a weaker invariant for a rare setup (FUSE, network shares), where a manual copy from the backup folder works today. It can be added later, with that invariant documented.
- **Tasks:** D5 (transaction, preflight, waits, rechecks), D14 (rules 2 and 3), D6 (undo of a restore).

#### M3-D25: whole-tree renames record stamp digests, not content hashes
- **Decision.** For every rename of a whole `WTF` tree, the `actions.jsonl` before and after digests use a new kind, `stamp:sha256:<hex>`: SHA-256 over the sorted `(path, kind, size, mode, mtime_ns)` of the tree. That covers the exchange, the move into the snapshot, undo's steps and recovery's preservation moves of a whole tree.
  - **A new type.** `TreeDigest` always renders `tree:sha256:` (`mutate.rs:177-180`), so a separate `StampDigest` type renders `stamp:sha256:`. `MutateOpts` gains `stamp_before/stamp_after: Option<StampDigest>`; when set, fsx takes them instead of content-hashing the tree.
  - **Which tree each digest describes.** The staged tree's digest is taken by a stat walk of the **staged copy** after the clone (copies get new mtimes). The live tree's is taken before the lock. Neither is re-verified under the lock.
  - **A guard.** A debug assertion in `restore.rs` checks that every directory rename in a restore or undo-of-restore session carries both stamps, so none falls back to hashing under the lock.
- **Why.**
  - A transaction session would otherwise content-hash the whole `WTF/` twice under the lock (§2.4 item 6): seconds for 500 MB, against a budget of 50 ms (D24).
  - Journal identity uses inodes and birth times, never digests (comment 653). The digests are diagnostic evidence for the M4 doctor, and a stamp digest is honest evidence of "which tree".
- **Rejected:** content digests computed before the lock. That is 0.5–1 s per restore for no safety gain.
- **Tasks:** D5 (and recorded on the vision, since it touches the doctor contract's `before_hash` semantics).

#### M3-D26: a whole restore keeps the current `WTF/` as a backup too
- **Decision.** Before staging, a whole restore creates a `before_restore` backup of the current `WTF/` (the same create path, no lock), on filesystems that can reflink. Elsewhere it skips that step and warns `before_restore_skipped`: the transaction snapshot still holds the old tree until retention.
  - Creating it runs **no backup retention**, so the backup being restored can never be pruned by the restore's own backup.
  - The restore holds a reader reservation on its source from plan to commit (M3-D48), so no other process's prune can remove it either.
  - Retention runs once, after the restore commits, with the source backup pinned for that pass.
  - Its history line is appended in the restore's commit window.
- **Why.**
  - Transaction retention prunes `WTF.previous` after 24 h, once 10 newer transactions exist or after 7 days (vision §5.5 retention).
  - A `before_restore` backup is listed and prunable like any other, so the pre-restore state survives a busy week. On btrfs it costs nothing.
- **Tasks:** D8.

#### M3-D27: a partial restore is a SavedVariables-only transaction that undo already understands
- **Decision.** `backup restore <id> --addon <A>…` restores the `<Folder>.lua` and `.lua.bak` files of addon A's folders under every account and character, as recorded in the backup's manifest.
  0. **Which folders** (no lock). The scope comes from **capture-time ownership** and is cross-checked against the present:
     - A name found in the backup's `addons.json` uses the folders it owned **then**. That still works after the addon was removed, or changed its folders since.
     - A name missing from `addons.json` (an older backup, an unmanaged addon) uses the target record's folders now, and the dry run says so.
     - A bare folder name present in the manifest selects just that folder.
     - **Ambiguity refuses rather than broadens.** A capture-time folder of A that another managed addon owns now is refused with `ref_ambiguous`. Its alternatives name each folder as `--addon <folder>` argv, and the user picks. A folder A owns now but did not own at capture is left alone, and the dry run lists it as "not in this backup; left as it is". Nothing outside the selected folders is touched.
     - **Version context.** The dry run and the result carry `{addon, captured_version, installed_version}`, shown as "settings written by WeakAuras 5.19.2; installed now: 5.20.0". omaddons never judges compatibility; addons migrate their own settings.
  1. **Prestage** (no lock):
     - copy those files from the backup into `<meta>/stage/<tx>/WTF/<rel>`;
     - hash them and the live files (there are few);
     - write a pre-restore `SvManifest` (`path`, live SHA-256 or `null`).
  2. **Under the lock:** `prepared` (kind `restore`, `writes_wtf: true`, with per-file staged stamps, in a `Writer::BackupRestore` session).
     - **Undo data first:** write `<meta>/snapshots/<tx>/WTF.manifest.json` (the pre-restore manifest) and run `snapshot_state` **before the first rename**, as the existing commits order it.
     - Recovery follows M3-D24 (b) and (c): rollback, waiting while the client runs, leaving unexpected live files untouched, and preserving displaced files through the journaled intent.
     - Steps:
       - Exchange staged ⇄ live for each file present in both;
       - Noreplace staged → live for files absent now;
       - Noreplace live → `stage/<tx>/WTF/<rel>` for live files the backup does not have (created since);
       - then Noreplace `stage/<tx>/WTF` → `<meta>/snapshots/<tx>/WTF`. The stage now holds the pre-restore originals, so this becomes the snapshot undo restores from.
     - **The same preflight as a whole restore** runs first: the stage on the client's mount, plus the exchange probe. Each candidate file's parent directory (account-wide and per character) must also have the stage's mount id, because single files move between them. On a filesystem without `RENAME_EXCHANGE` (FUSE, network shares), a partial restore is refused with `filesystem_unsupported` before anything is copied, exactly as a whole one is.
       - The first draft's per-file two-rename fallback was dropped. It would have left a file absent for a moment, which the game reads as "reset this addon", and mixed two snapshot layouts in one transaction.
       - README Limitations names the workaround for those filesystems: with the game closed, copy the files from `<meta>/backups/<id>/WTF/` by hand, a plain directory.
  3. **Commit:** `swapped`, record, history with one op per folder: `{"op":"saved_variables","folder":"<F>","addon":"<name or F>","files":N}`. `FolderOp::SavedVariables` serializes as `saved_variables` (an explicit serde rename, because `FolderOp` is `rename_all = "lowercase"`). Then `committed`.

  The result is exactly the layout `engine::undo::plan_saved_variables` restores from. **Undo of a partial restore is the existing SavedVariables undo**: files changed since are restored, and files the restore created are moved aside. `sv_skip` applies (symlinked or two-spelled folders are skipped, `saved_variables_out_of_scope`).
  - **For that undo to be undoable in turn,** a `saved_variables` op's folder joins undo's `touched` set (`undo.rs:897-899`), so the undo snapshots that folder's SavedVariables with a manifest. It joins with no folder swap, and the undo's history records a `saved_variables` op for it.
  - `FolderPlan::inverse` and `restored_state` must not treat it as a changed addon record (`undo.rs:1088-1092`).
  - A `wtf` op is excluded from `touched`; D6 plans it.
- **Why.** Undo's SavedVariables code is the most carefully crash-tested code in the tree (comments 640, 645, 692, 701). Reusing its on-disk layout means undo of a partial restore inherits all of it.
- **Rejected:** restoring the files directly with `sv_restore` payload semantics. Roll-forward would then have to write SavedVariables after `swapped`, which defers awkwardly when the client starts in between. Journaled steps before `swapped` roll back cleanly, with M3-D24 (c)'s rules.
- **Tasks:** D7.

#### M3-D28: undo and restores conflict where they would overwrite each other
- **Decision.** Conflict detection (`check_conflicts`) learns two ops:
  - `wtf` touches the whole `WTF/`;
  - `saved_variables` touches folder F's SavedVariables.

  The rules:
  1. Undo of a whole restore R conflicts with any later transaction that wrote SavedVariables: an undo with a SavedVariables restore, a partial restore, another whole restore. The fix names the newest of them to undo first.
  2. Undo of any transaction T whose snapshot has a SavedVariables manifest, after a later whole restore R, is `undo_conflict` unless `--saved-variables keep` (folders only). The fix names R, with the `keep` command as the alternative. The same check applies to the deferred follow-up `undo T --saved-variables restore` (`check_conflicts(…, Some(by))`, `undo.rs:694`).
  3. A partial restore P conflicts like a folder op on F's SavedVariables, in both directions.
  4. Undo of a whole restore restores the pre-restore tree. It stages `snapshots/<R>/WTF.previous` → exchange → the current tree goes to `snapshots/<undo>/WTF.previous`, so the undo is itself undoable.
     - It runs in a `BackupRestore` session with `writes_wtf: true`, with the same topology preflight and the same no-fallback rule as M3-D24.
     - Because it reverts every play session since R, its dry run (and the widget's "Undo last" confirm) reports `changed_since`: the files whose size or mtime differ from the restored backup's manifest.
  5. **Unreadable history fails closed** (M3-D45). A history line this binary cannot decode, newer than the transaction T being undone, **is assumed to touch everything it might**.
     - When the line is valid JSON, its raw `target` and `ops[].folder` strings are read as `serde_json::Value`. A line on another target is ignored. A line on T's target is treated as writing **all** SavedVariables of that target and the folders it names. It is treated as writing every folder when it names none, or names `WTF`.
     - A line that is not even JSON is treated as touching every target.
     - The ordinary rules then apply. A SavedVariables restore is refused with `undo_conflict`, `details.reason: "history_unreadable"` and the line count. The alternative is `--saved-variables keep`, offered only when the line's folders are disjoint from T's. A folder overlap is refused outright. The fix is prose: "a newer omaddons wrote that history; undo it with that version".
- **Why.** Without rule 2, undoing an old install after a restore would overwrite the restored SavedVariables with the install's week-old copies. That is technically "undo", but it is exactly the data loss backups exist to prevent. Rule 5 closes the same hole for history this binary cannot read, which is how M2 binaries fall into it (§2.9).
- **Tasks:** D6, D7, A3.

#### M3-D29: restores never run while the client runs
- **Decision.** Whole and partial restores are refused while the target's client runs, or while running is unknown. The refusal is `game_running` with `details.reason: "saved_variables"`, through `PolicyOp::RestoreSavedVariables`. `--while-running` does not lift it, under any `running_policy`.
  - Running is checked at plan time, again under the lock as the last step before the journal, and again before any in-process recovery (M3-D24 (c) 1).
  - **It is a refusal check, not exclusion.** The game takes no omaddons lock, so a launch in the milliseconds between the last check and the exchange cannot be prevented. README states this residual race and its consequence: the game may write its in-memory settings over the restored files at logout, and the undo snapshot keeps the pre-restore tree.
- **Why.** D33: SavedVariables are never written while the client runs, because it overwrites them on logout. Stating what the check cannot do is part of the promise (review finding).
- **Tasks:** D5, D7, D8.
