comments.text:
**Decision log, part 4 of 5: backups (M3-D30 to M3-D36, M3-D43), triage and contract (M3-D37 to M3-D42) (M3 plan, 2026-10-21).**

Each decision gives what was decided, why, the alternatives rejected, and which tasks carry it out. Decisions marked **departure** change what the vision bead body or a later vision comment says; G2 (`omad-m3-widget-errors-backups-7qmx.7.2`) records each one as a vision comment. The one marked **owner-visible** (M3-D30) changes a README promise, and plan approval approved it. Decisions are numbered by when they were made, not by topic, so the topic groups below interleave (M3-D43 and M3-D44 were added before the third review, M3-D45 to M3-D48 in the third review).

Section labels (`§x.y`) and plan keys (A1 … G3) are resolved by the milestone epic body ("How to read the M3 beads") and the key → id comment. Code references are as of `af10e34`.

#### M3-D30 (owner-visible): `auto_backup` defaults to `daily`
- **Decision.** `auto_backup` takes `off | daily | daily-copy`, and the default becomes **`daily`**.
  - `daily` makes automatic backups (M3-D31) only by cloning. It uses `ClonePolicy::Required` at the fsx primitive: an unsupported clone returns `NotReflinkable` from the FICLONE attempt itself and **never enters the byte-copy branch** (§2.4 item 8). The automatic backup then stops at its first file, having copied zero payload bytes, and that is not an error.
  - `daily-copy` also makes byte copies (`ClonePolicy::Preferred`, today's behaviour), within the byte-copy budget of M3-D48.
  - **Capability is observed, not assumed.** `statfs` on `<meta>` is only an **eligibility hint**. btrfs (`0x9123683E`) and xfs (`0x58465342`) are worth an attempt; anything else (ext4 `0xEF53`, tmpfs, FUSE, NTFS) is `unsupported` without one, and nothing is written. Each attempt records its outcome per target in the backup inventory projection (M3-D37): `supported` after a successful clone, `unsupported` after `NotReflinkable`, with the time and result. An xfs without reflink therefore shows as unsupported after its first attempt, instead of appearing to work forever.
  - **`status` reports configured and observed separately:** `backups.auto = {mode, capability: unknown|supported|unsupported, last: {at, result} | null}`. `result` is `created`, `unchanged`, `done_today`, `no_reflink`, `space_low`, `in_progress`, `running`, `failed`, `off` or `no_wtf`.
  - **The stale-backup recommendation**, whatever the mode: `status` recommends `omaddons backup create -t <id>` when that target's newest **qualifying** capture (M3-D31) is older than `BACKUP_STALE_AFTER` (7 days), or when there is none, provided its `WTF/` holds SavedVariables. A freshly imported old archive, a partial recovered backup or a best-effort capture does not silence it. There is nothing to protect on a never-played client.
  - The statfs hint means a `daily` attempt on an ext4 filesystem writes nothing at all. Tests pin the answer with a debug-only seam (`OMADDONS_FS_CLONE`, D1), so suites stay deterministic on any `TMPDIR`.
- **Why.**
  - Defaults decide outcomes. With `off`, almost nobody gets the protection M3 exists to give.
  - On copy-on-write filesystems (btrfs, which Omarchy uses; xfs with reflink) a backup costs milliseconds when made, and space only in proportion to what the game rewrites afterwards. Retention and the space guard bound that (M3-D32, M3-D48).
  - On ext4 a byte copy of a 300 MB `WTF/` every day would surprise, so it requires explicit opt-in.
  - A clone-only policy that can still pay for a full byte copy of a large first file is not clone-only (review finding). And a mode reported as "on" that never succeeds would be a lie.
- **README change.** `auto_backup` now defaults to `daily`, with a new value `daily-copy`. README promised "default `off`; used from milestone 3". By the house rules a change to a README promise needs the owner, and **approving this plan approves it**. If the owner rejects it, change one constant: the default becomes `off`, and the recommendation text stays.
- **Rejected:**
  - (i) Keeping `off`: the protection would not reach the users who need it.
  - (ii) `daily` with byte copies everywhere: surprising disk use.
  - (iii) A separate boolean `auto_backup_copy`: two keys for one choice.
- **Departure.** It changes the vision §5.6 default. G2 records it.
- **Tasks:** D3.

#### M3-D31: when automatic backups happen: two triggers, qualifying checkpoints, coalescing
- **Decision.**
  - **A qualifying capture** is a backup of this target with kind `manual`, `auto` or `before_restore`, not `partial`, with `consistency: stable`, captured on this machine. Imported, recovered and best-effort backups never qualify. They are kept, listed and restorable, but they say nothing about whether today's settings are protected. Scheduling and the stale recommendation use the qualifying capture's `captured_at`, never a directory's age, a publish time or an imported source's date.
  - **(a) Pre-change checkpoint.** In `engine::tx::commit_target`, after the in-flight lock and before `stage_all`, and in `engine::undo` before `stage_trees`. Both points run without the global lock, only for targets that will commit, and never on a dry run or a no-op.
    - Only transactions that move folders or write SavedVariables trigger it: install, update, remove, sync, copy, undo. Not `adopt` or `pin` (records only), and not settings commands.
    - **At most one a local day:** it is due only when no `auto` backup with `trigger: pre_change` has a `captured_at` in today's local day (`jiff::tz::TimeZone::system()`). A restore's own `before_restore` backup (M3-D26) counts as that day's pre-change checkpoint.
    - It runs even while the client runs. SavedVariables on disk only change at logout and `/reload`, so the copy is of a settled state, and `client_running: true` is recorded.
  - **(b) Post-session checkpoint.** `omaddons backup create --auto [-t T]` is the after-play trigger.
    - It skips a target whose client runs, or whose running state is unknown (`running`): a session that has not ended has not written its settings.
    - It is **not** limited to one a day. A player's second session of the evening is worth its own checkpoint, and retention thins them later (M3-D32).
    - The widget runs it when a target's client goes from running to not running, and for every stopped target at service startup (M3-D13). So protection does not depend on the shell having seen the transition.
    - There is no daemon: the triggers are the widget's own doorbells.
  - **Coalescing, for both triggers.** A capture is skipped as `unchanged` when the live `WTF/` inventory equals the newest qualifying capture's manifest: same paths, kinds, sizes and mtimes, from one read-only stat walk of a few milliseconds. Repeated triggers with nothing played make no duplicates.
  - **One at a time per target.** The due check, the capture and the publication run under the target's backup scheduling lock (M3-D48). A second trigger that finds it held skips as `in_progress`, so two commands at once make one backup.
  - **Space first.** Before capturing, the space guard of M3-D48 runs, and it may skip as `space_low`.
  - **Outcome.** A skip is a success with its reason (`--dry-run` reports the decision). A failure warns `auto_backup_failed` (the transaction goes ahead) and is retried by the next trigger. Every outcome is recorded in the inventory projection, which feeds `status`'s `backups.auto.last`.
  - **History.** A target registered only by this transaction gets its backup's history line written in the commit window, after registration (M3-D33).
- **Why.**
  - "Before the day's first mutation" (vision §5.8) gives one restore point per day from before omaddons touched anything. The post-session checkpoint protects against what players actually lose settings to: the game, and addons that reset their database on load. A good session's state is captured before the next, possibly bad, one.
  - The first draft's single daily bucket, keyed on "the newest backup of any kind", let a morning pre-update backup suppress the evening's capture. It also let an import of a year-old archive count as today's protection (review finding).
  - Outside the lock it keeps D24.
  - Records-only changes cannot hurt `WTF/`.
- **Rejected:** one automatic backup per day of any trigger (the first draft); post-session captures while the client runs; a timer in the widget.
- **Tasks:** D3, F8.

#### M3-D32: backup retention
- **Decision.** After every backup create, automatic backup and restore, a per-target retention pass runs (`src/backup/prune.rs`). It keeps:
  - every backup younger than `BACKUP_MIN_AGE` (24 h);
  - the **newest qualifying capture**, whatever its age (M3-D31);
  - for each of the newest `BACKUP_AUTO_KEEP_DAYS` local days that hold any automatic backup (7, config `limits.backup_auto_keep_days`), that day's **first** `pre_change` backup, its **last** `post_session` backup, and every `before_restore` backup;
  - every `manual`, `imported` or `recovered` backup. A recovered one holds a play session, and the others are the user's.

  It prunes every other automatic backup: same-day extras older than 24 h, and days beyond the window. The count is bounded: at most the last 24 hours' captures, plus two per kept day, plus that window's restores.
  - **Space pressure** adds one reclamation pass, never touching the protections above. It is defined in M3-D48.
  - `backup prune` without ids runs the same pass. With `--keep N` (the newest N of **each** kind stay) or `--older-than D` it also prunes manual, imported and recovered backups, but never one younger than 24 h and never the newest qualifying capture. `backup prune <id>…` removes exactly the named ones; the 24 h protection is lifted there because the request is explicit.
  - **Busy backups.** A backup held by a reader reservation (a restore, export or verify in progress, M3-D48) is skipped and reported as `busy`, never deleted under its reader.
  - **Deletion** goes through `fsx::prune(PruneReason::BackupPrune)`. `src/backup/prune.rs` joins `PRUNE_CALLERS`.
  - **Sizes** shown are apparent bytes, labelled "apparent; initially shared copy-on-write" when reflinked, next to the filesystem's measured free space (M3-D48). omaddons never claims a backup's exclusive physical size, which reflinks make unknowable without a full extent walk.
- **Why.**
  - Automatic backups must be bounded, or a heavy WeakAuras user's SavedVariables churn (about 20 MB rewritten per session) grows forever. Two triggers make a per-day rule the natural bound, where a bare count of 7 would cover only two or three days for a player with several sessions a day.
  - What the user created explicitly is theirs to delete.
- **Tasks:** D4.

#### M3-D33: backups in history, and registration
- **Decision.**
  - Each backup appends a `HistoryEntry` of kind `backup` (`ops: []`) with a new optional field, `backup: {id, kind, files, bytes}`. It is never undoable (`TxKind::Backup.is_undoable() == false`, already true), and `undo` steps over it like settings lines.
  - `backup create` on an unregistered target registers it under the global lock (`LockedRegistry::ensure_registered`), as engine commits do, then appends the line.
  - Pruned backups append nothing; the files are the record.
- **Why.** Attribution (vision §5.9: every change records actor, reason, argv), and `history` shows backups in order.
- **Tasks:** D2, D3.

#### M3-D34: `backup export` writes a new file, never replaces one
- **Decision.** `backup export <id> <file>` streams a deterministic `tar` (sorted, uid/gid 0, the original mtimes and modes) through `zstd` level 3. The archive holds:
  - `backup.json`;
  - `WTF/…`;
  - `manifest.json`, now **with SHA-256 per file**. It is written **last**, after the hashes were computed while the `WTF/` entries streamed. Import stages everything first and verifies against it before anything leaves the stage.
    - When the local manifest already has hashes (a `--verify` capture, an import, a verified baseline, M3-D47), each streamed file is compared with them. A mismatch aborts the export with `hash_mismatch` ("backup … is damaged") and removes the partial temporary file.
    - The archive's `backup.json` records the hashes' provenance: `verified_against: capture|import|later`, or `computed_at_export` when there were none.

  **Streaming, with no intermediate copy.** The tar+zstd producer runs on a scoped thread and hands bytes over a bounded channel to fsx's reader-content `WriteFile` (DEC-11). fsx writes **directly into its hidden temporary sibling of `<file>`**, which is on the destination's own filesystem. Then it finishes the encoder, fsyncs the file, publishes with no-clobber semantics (`Expect::Absent`, `persist_noclobber`), and fsyncs the destination directory. Mode 0600.
  - A producer error, a disk-full or a crash removes only this operation's unpublished temporary file. The published file appears complete or not at all.
  - Nothing is staged in `<cache>`, so an export needs no cache capacity and writes the compressed bytes once.
  - **Scope.** fsx gets a **runtime single-path scope**: `ScopeTable::with_export_file(<file>)` admits exactly that path, plus its temp sibling, for `Writer::Backup`. No such scope exists today (§2.3). It requires an existing parent directory. It refuses paths inside any discovered client dir, any Wine prefix (an ancestor holding `drive_c/` and `dosdevices/`), and omaddons' config, state and cache dirs.
  - The export holds a reader reservation on its backup for the whole stream (M3-D48).
  - **An existing `<file>`** fails with the new error `file_exists` (exit 4, not retryable, prose fix "choose another file name, or delete that file yourself").
  - **No stdout.** `<file>` must be a path; `-` is a usage error ("write the export to a file"). Binary data on stdout would break the one-envelope rule under `--json`.
- **Why.**
  - A same-disk copy does not survive a disk failure (vision §5.8).
  - Never replacing a file makes export safe to script.
  - A narrow runtime scope keeps the single-writer and scope guarantees, in the M2-D19 spirit (no general `--output`).
  - Streaming straight to the destination's temp sibling writes the archive once and needs no cache space. The first draft wrote it to `<cache>/tmp` and then copied it, which doubled the I/O (review finding).
- **Tasks:** D9.

#### M3-D35: `backup import` exists, and accepts only an exact archive
- **Decision.** `backup import <file.tar.zst> -t T` validates the archive the way archive inspection validates zips, and more strictly, because the archive is a tree omaddons wrote itself:
  - **Entry types.** Only the header types omaddons' exporter writes are accepted: regular files, directories, symlinks, and the GNU long-name and PAX path headers the `tar` crate uses for long paths. Hard links, devices, FIFOs, sparse files, multivolume and every other type are refused, before extraction, with `unsafe_archive` and `details.reason: "unsupported_entry"`.
  - **Names.** No absolute paths, `..`, drive letters, control characters, duplicates or case-folded collisions. A path is at most `BACKUP_IMPORT_MAX_PATH` (4,096 bytes), and per-entry metadata (PAX and long-name records) at most `BACKUP_IMPORT_MAX_META_BYTES` (64 KiB).
  - **Metadata objects.** Exactly one `backup.json`, exactly one `manifest.json` and at most one `addons.json`, each bounded by `DISCOVERY_FILE_MAX_BYTES`.
  - **Bounds.** `BACKUP_IMPORT_MAX_ENTRIES`, `BACKUP_IMPORT_MAX_BYTES`, `ARCHIVE_MAX_RATIO` past `ARCHIVE_RATIO_FLOOR`, and a zstd decoder window of at most `2^BACKUP_IMPORT_MAX_WINDOW_LOG` (`Decoder::window_log_max`, 24, i.e. 16 MiB). A larger window is `bad_archive`, `details.reason: "decoder_window"`, so a crafted frame cannot demand gigabytes of decoder memory.
  - **An exact set match.** The validated manifest and the payload must be a bijection. Every payload entry is listed in the manifest with the same path, kind, size, mode and link target. Every manifest entry is present in the payload, and every regular file's SHA-256 matches. An unlisted payload entry, a missing one, or any difference is `unsafe_archive` (`details.reason: "manifest_mismatch"`), with the first offending path passed through the archive's path redactor (M3-D21).
  - **Symlinks.** Only relative links that resolve inside the backup's `WTF/` (else `unsafe_archive`, `details.reason: "symlink_escape"`), since exports keep a tree's symlinks.
    - **No extraction write ever follows an archive-provided symlink.** Regular files and directories are extracted first, each with `O_NOFOLLOW` semantics through fsx.
    - The link graph is then validated: every target is inside, resolved without following other links, and acyclic.
    - Links are materialized last.

  Entries are extracted into `<meta>/stage/<tx>/backup/`, verified as above, and only then renamed into `backups/<new id>`. They get kind `imported`, `captured_at` from the source, and `source: {id, target_id, family, created_at, captured_at, tool_version}` copied from the archive's `backup.json`. `integrity` becomes `verified` with `baseline: import`, because every hash was just checked (M3-D47). A family that differs from the target's is refused with `wrong_flavor` (exit 4), unless `--force`.
- **Why.** An export that only `tar -x` can restore bypasses undo and the running guard. With import, "survive a disk failure" is a two-command story.
  - "Every file hash matches" alone would not be enough: an unlisted file, a duplicate metadata object, or a symlink parent created earlier in the archive could still put bytes where they do not belong (review finding). A bijection plus links-last closes each of those.
- **Departure.** The vision listed create, list, restore, export and prune. G2 records the addition.
- **Tasks:** D10.

#### M3-D36: `tar` and `zstd` crates
- **Decision.** Add `tar` (default features off) and `zstd` (default features; it compiles the C zstd library through `cc`, as `ring` already compiles C). Run `argc gate --all` (cargo deny) in the bead that adds them. Both licenses (MIT/Apache, BSD) are on the `deny.toml` list.
- **Why.** The vision named them (vision §5.12 crates). They are the standard choices, and `ruzstd`'s encoder is not mature.
- **Tasks:** D9.

#### M3-D43: `backup create` defaults to every live client that has a `WTF/`
- **Decision.** Without `-t`, `backup create` backs up every **live** target whose `WTF/` exists, each as its own backup and history line, all under one run. Test clients are included only with `-t`.
- **Why.** "Back up everything" is the first guess. It mirrors `update` and `sync` (family sections never touch test clients).
- **Tasks:** D2.

### Triage and contract

#### M3-D37: `status` grows triage blocks the widget and agents share
- **Decision.** Additive keys (DEC-4), specified in §7.2:
  - `data.summary`: `{targets, running[], updates{available, targets}, issues{p0,p1,p2,p3}, errors{new, targets}, check_due, widget_outdated, state}`, where `state` is `attention|errors|updates|idle`, in that priority;
  - `data.last_change`: the newest undoable run, `{run, kind, at, actor, reason, targets[], changes{added,replaced,removed,recorded,restored}, undo{command, argv}}` or `null`, with `data.last_change_state` (`ok|unknown`). `undo` is `omaddons undo --run <run>`;
  - `data.widget`: `{omarchy, installed, enabled, version, outdated, context_matches}` or `null` when Omarchy is absent;
  - `targets[].issues[]`: `{id, severity, title, addon, remediation{command, argv, destructive}}`, one per existing attention reason. Drift reasons get one per addon, from `drift`. `addon_degraded` gets one per target with a count, because `StatusTarget` carries only the degraded count. The mapping table is in §7.2. Ids are vision D20 `fm-…` failure-mode ids (body revision 2, vision §5.8 catalog), so M4's doctor findings extend them;
  - `targets[].errors` (B7) and `targets[].backups` (D11).

  `attention[]` stays unchanged. `issues[]` is its structured twin.
- **Bounded work: `status --cached` reads projections, never unbounded authority.** The 5 ms promise must not stretch over an unbounded history, unlimited manual backups and every account directory. So the two expensive answers come from **small, rebuildable projections**, each tagged with what it covers:
  - **`<cache>/history_tail.json`** (kind `history_tail`, 1.0, A2). It holds every history line from the start of the oldest of the newest `HISTORY_TAIL_RUNS` (16) runs **that contain an undoable entry**, verbatim and grouped by run id, so backup-only and settings-only runs can never push the last undoable run out. It also holds `covers: {from, bytes, last_line_sha256}`: the byte range of `history.jsonl` it reflects, and its last line. The projection is capped at `HISTORY_TAIL_MAX_BYTES` (1 MiB); past the cap it keeps only the newest runs that fit and lets `select` answer `NeedsOlder`.
    - It is updated inside `history::append_line`, the one function both `append` and `append_setting` use (`src/state/history.rs:218`), under the caller's lock, after the line is durable. So every appender maintains it, settings lines included, with no new call sites for the incremental update.
    - `status --cached` checks `covers.bytes` against one `stat` of `history.jsonl`. A match lets it run the **same run-selection function `undo` uses** (`src/app/undo.rs:355-416`, made pure and shared) over those lines. That stays correct when runs interleave (§2.4 item 14).
    - A mismatch, a missing file, or a selection that needs older lines than the projection holds gives `last_change: null` with `last_change_state: "unknown"`. A fast but incomplete answer is worse than an explicit "unknown".
    - A failed projection write never fails the append. An append that finds `covers` stale only marks it so; the rebuild from the whole history runs **after the caller releases the global lock** (a 20 MB history must not stretch the 50 ms lock-hold budget), from exactly one place: the dispatch epilogue in `src/app/mod.rs`, which calls `history_tail::rebuild_if_stale(paths)` after every command that mutates. When the projection is fresh, that costs one `stat`. A concurrent append can make it stale again, and `covers` catches that. Plain `status` computes `last_change` from the full history and writes nothing.
  - **`<cache>/backups.json`** (kind `backup_inventory`, 1.0, D1). Per target key it holds counts by kind, apparent bytes, the newest qualifying capture, the newest backup, the `auto` capability and last attempt (M3-D30), plus `covers`: the sorted ids it reflects.
    - It is rewritten by every command that changes `backups/`: create, auto, import, prune, verify, and recovery's preservation.
    - `status --cached` validates it with one `read_dir` of `<meta>/backups/`. The same id set means it is current. A different set gives the projection's numbers marked `stale: true`, with the listing's count, and `backup list` (or any backup command) rebuilds it.
    - `backup list` itself reads only `backup.json` files, never whole trees (M3-D47).
  - **Errors** already work this way (the memo, M3-D20), and their probes are bounded by M3-D44.
  - A projection is derived. Deleting it costs one "unknown" until the next writer, and never correctness.
- **Why.**
  - The bar needs severity ("urgent on P0/P1", vision §5.11), error counts and "undo last" in one ≤ 5 ms call.
  - Agents benefit equally: `summary.state` is a one-key "anything to do?".
  - Using the doctor's ids now avoids a breaking change at the M4 freeze.
  - The first draft read a 64 KiB history tail and summed backup sizes from one `read_dir`. Neither could be right: a tail cannot prove it holds a whole interleaved run, and a directory listing holds no sizes (review finding).
- **Rejected:**
  - (i) Severities on `attention` strings: a type change.
  - (ii) Computing severity in QML: logic in the view (D2 of the vision).
  - (iii) A database or daemon for these summaries: two small JSON files with a validity check are enough.
- **Tasks:** A2, B7, D1, D11, E4.

#### M3-D38: widget installs are recorded in history
- **Decision.**
  - A new settings kind, `TxKind::Widget` (`is_setting() == true`), for `omarchy install` and `omarchy remove`.
  - `Scope::History` admits `Writer::Omarchy`. `omarchy install` and `remove` take the global lock briefly (recovering first, comment 723) to swap and append.
  - **Omarchy scope roots.** `<plugins>/omaddons` and each install's stage are scope roots, and fsx refuses any non-`CreateDir` access at a root (`scope.rs:343`), so every swap and prune would fail.
    - Their rows accept `Rename` (both directions) from `Writer::Omarchy`.
    - **Every install owns its stage:** `<plugins>/.omaddons.stage-<ulid>`, where the ULID is the operation's id, never one fixed `.omaddons.stage`.
      - The operation holds an `InflightLock` (`create`, in `<state>/inflight/`, §2.4 item 15) from allocating the stage until it publishes.
      - A stage is reclaimed only by a process that can take that stage's lock. Elapsed time is never ownership evidence.
      - Two installers, a terminal one and the widget's self-reinstall, can therefore never prune or mix each other's files.
    - Two hidden rows join them: `<plugins>/.omaddons.old-<ulid>`, for the fallback swap and for remove, and `<plugins>/.omaddons.trash`, the prune trash for this side, so `fsx::prune` can rename victims there.
    - Hidden names are invisible to Omarchy's registry and hot reload (§2.5).
    - These are scope-table changes, recorded on the vision.
  - **Under the global lock**, an install re-reads the installed `Build.js` identity before publishing. If a competing install or remove changed it since staging, it rechecks idempotence: unchanged rendered bytes mean `unchanged`; otherwise it publishes its own validated stage. A remove that finds the plugin already gone reports `not_found`. History names the operation that published.
- **Why.** Every change is attributed (vision §5.9). The widget's self-reinstall shows up as `actor: widget`. A fixed shared stage dir assembled outside the lock let two installers delete or mix each other's files before either reached the atomic swap (review finding). The engine already solved this for transactions with in-flight locks, so widget installs reuse that.
- **Tasks:** E2, E3.

#### M3-D39: help layout
- **Decision.**
  - Look gains `errors` after `search`; the line wraps to a continuation line, which `render_groups` supports.
  - Change gains `backup` after `undo`.
  - Setup gains `omarchy` before `help`.
  - Bare help stays under 30 lines and 80 columns.
  - `tests/cli_skeleton.rs` and the `help.rs` layout test are updated by the tasks that add each command. The title line gains "and an Omarchy widget" (the `cli.rs:29` comment).
- **Tasks:** B6, D1, E2.

#### M3-D40: a new progress phase, `copy`
- **Decision.** `Phase::Copy` (`"copy"`), emitted by the shared tree clone (backup create, restore staging), verify, export and import. Its `current`/`total` count files.
  - Its `message` is a fixed label such as `"WTF/ files"` or `"verifying"`, **never a path**: every path below `WTF/Account/` names an account, a realm and a character (M3-D21). The widget shows that message.
- **Why.** These are the new long operations. `stage` means archive staging today, and reusing it would mislead.
- **Tasks:** D1 (adds the phase with the tree clone), D2, D5, D9, D10, D13.

#### M3-D41: widget tests run in the gate when the widget changes
- **Decision.**
  - `omarchy/tests/` holds `*.test.js` for `Model.js`, run with `bun test`, and `qml/tst_*.qml` with mocks under `qml/imports/` (`Quickshell/Io/{Process, StdioCollector, SplitParser, IpcHandler}`, `Quickshell/Hyprland`, `qs/Commons`, `qs/Ui` minimal stubs), run with `QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen QT_QUICK_BACKEND=software qmltestrunner -input omarchy/tests/qml -import omarchy/tests/qml/imports`. This is the hey plugin's harness (§2.5).
  - **One ordered pipeline**, run by `scripts/gate.sh` after `cargo test`, with every artifact generated fresh into one temporary directory (`OMADDONS_WIDGET_OUT`). Nothing generated is committed or read from the tree:
    1. **Envelopes:** `cargo test --test omarchy_widget -- --ignored write_widget_fixtures` writes real-binary envelopes for every reducer scenario;
    2. **Model and argv:** `bun test omarchy/tests` runs the reducers over those envelopes, and writes `built-argv.json` from the actual `Model.buildArgv` and `Model.classifyCliArgv`;
    3. **Argv contract:** `cargo test --test omarchy_widget -- --ignored validate_built_argv` parses exactly those argv with `Cli::try_parse_from` (M3-D2). Rust never fills a template slot itself;
    4. **QML:** copy `omarchy/` into `$OMADDONS_WIDGET_OUT/plugin/` together with a fixture `Build.js`, and run `qmltestrunner` over the copy's `tests/qml`. `Service.qml` imports `"Build.js"` relative to its own directory, and that file is generated at install, so a mock under `-import` cannot stand in for it. The copy is what makes a clean checkout pass.
  - **When each runs.** Steps 1–3 are cheap (seconds) and run on **every** gate. A CLI change, a clap flag or an envelope key, can break the widget as surely as a QML edit can. Step 4 runs when a changed file is under `omarchy/`, or with `--all`.
  - A missing `bun` (needed always) or `qmltestrunner` (needed for step 4) fails with a clear message. A clean checkout with no generated files must pass.
  - `Model.js` ends with `if (typeof module !== "undefined") module.exports = {…}` so bun can `require` it.
  - `qmllint` runs at checkpoints (G3), with zero errors required and warnings recorded.
- **Why.** QML logic is otherwise untested until a human looks at the bar. The harness is proven on this machine. bun follows the house JavaScript rule.
  - The first draft ran the Rust argv check inside `cargo test`, before bun had produced the file it reads. Another of its instructions substituted the slots again in Rust, which tests a second implementation rather than the real one (review finding).
- **Tasks:** F1, F2.

#### M3-D42: the widget checks it matches the binary
- **Decision.** On every status envelope, the service compares:
  - `schema_version` major with `1`, and
  - `tool_version` with `Build.TOOL_VERSION`.

  A mismatch puts the service in an **incompatible, read-only state**:
  - it keeps the last compatible summary, marked stale;
  - it clears every pending confirmation;
  - it stops automatic work (checks, `backup_auto`, errors refreshes);
  - it disables every template and remediation button;
  - it offers only **Retry** (re-run `status`) and **Reinstall widget**.

  `data.widget.outdated` (hash-based, M3-D7) is the same state: asset drift means the widget's templates may no longer match the binary.
  - **Recheck before dispatch.** Immediately before starting any mutation, the service checks that the last envelope it saw is compatible and that its context generation is unchanged. A confirmation given before a binary change or a reinstall can therefore never run afterwards.
  - The reinstall runs `[binary, "--actor", "widget", "--reason", "reinstall from the bar widget", "omarchy", "install"]` (standard flags first, as M3-D2 places them) in a `Process` with the stamped context and `startDetached()` (M3-D3). It is detached because the reload kills the service's own processes (vision §5.11).
- **Why.** "Keep rendering what it can" is fine for a stale summary, but no basis for executing fixes. A binary whose envelope the widget does not understand may give the same argv a different meaning (review finding). The project deliberately version-locks the widget, and this uses that boundary.
- **Tasks:** F2, E4.

comments.text:
**Decision log, part 5 of 5: safety contracts added after the third review, M3-D45 to M3-D48 (M3 plan, 2026-10-21).**

Each decision gives what was decided, why, the alternatives rejected, and which tasks carry it out. Decisions marked **departure** change what the vision bead body or a later vision comment says; G2 (`omad-m3-widget-errors-backups-7qmx.7.2`) records each one as a vision comment. The one marked **owner-visible** (M3-D30) changes a README promise, and plan approval approved it. Decisions are numbered by when they were made, not by topic, so the topic groups below interleave (M3-D43 and M3-D44 were added before the third review, M3-D45 to M3-D48 in the third review).

Section labels (`§x.y`) and plan keys (A1 … G3) are resolved by the milestone epic body ("How to read the M3 beads") and the key → id comment. Code references are as of `af10e34`.

### Safety contracts added after the third review

#### M3-D45: persisted formats fail closed
- **Decision.** M3 adds journal fields and line kinds (`writes_wtf`, `staged_stamp`, `staged_files`, `source_backup`, `preserve`, `preserved`), history op values (`wtf`, `saved_variables`) and fields (`backup`, `from`, `files`, `sv_restored`), history kinds (`widget`, `dismiss`) and state files. Every reader M3 touches therefore fails closed on what it cannot read:
  - **Journal version.** `recover_parsed` compares `Prepared.schema_version` with `journal::CURRENT` (§2.9: today it is never compared).
    - A newer **major** version is never recovered by this binary. The journal, its stage and its snapshots stay, the target reports `journal_pending` with `details.reason: "journal_too_new"`, and the fix is prose: "a newer omaddons started this change; finish it with that version".
    - A newer minor is recovered, ignoring unknown fields as today.
    - M3 writes journal `1.1`: `writes_wtf` journals and preservation lines are additive, and an M2 binary reading them is refused by scope at its first `WTF/` rename (§2.3).
  - **Unreadable lines are not "nothing to do".** A journal whose `prepared` line does not decode, or that holds any other complete line `parse` could not decode, is **never** treated as `Unprepared`. Recovery leaves the journal, its in-flight lock, its stage and its state-side snapshots in place, with `journal_pending` and `details.reason: "journal_unreadable"`, which is manual repair as in M2. That removes the latent M2 hazard where an undecodable `prepared` line led recovery to prune the journal and the transaction's snapshots (§2.9).
    - **A torn append is not unreadable.** A final fragment without its newline is a crash mid-append, and M2 already tolerates it (`journal.rs` tests `roll_forward_finds_its_own_line_that_lost_only_its_newline` and the next one). The journal is write-ahead, so the step it would have recorded never ran. It is ignored exactly as today. A journal that is nothing but a torn `prepared` fragment is pruned as today, because nothing ran.
    - `parse` therefore counts two things separately: `torn_tail` (0 or 1, tolerated) and `unknown_lines` (any complete undecodable line, fail closed).
  - **History.** `history` and `list` keep skipping unreadable lines with `history_lines_skipped`. **Undo's conflict analysis fails closed** instead: M3-D28 rule 5 assumes an unreadable line on the target touches everything it might.
  - **Early refusal of newer state.** Before planning any mutation of a target, the engine loads that target's record and files index, and the registry for a registration. If any is `VersionStatus::Newer`, it refuses with `state_too_new` **before staging**, instead of failing inside the commit window after folders moved (§2.9). That is the barrier every binary from M3 on honours.
  - **What M3 cannot fix.** An M2 binary (`af10e34` or older) has neither guard.
    - Run against state M3 wrote, it can read history without seeing restores. Its undo with `--saved-variables auto` would put an old transaction's SavedVariables copies back over restored ones.
    - It fails only late, at the record save, if the record is newer.
    - It is refused by scope if it tries to recover an M3 restore journal (§2.3).

    There is no pre-mutation structure that M2 already refuses, because M2's refusals happen after side effects. So M3 **does not claim a downgrade barrier against M2**. It documents the limit in README Limitations ("do not run a pre-M3 build against state M3 has written; reading with it is safe"), and D12 characterizes the real af10e34 binary against committed and interrupted M3 restores, recording exactly what it refuses and what it would do.
- **Why.** The review asked for a downgrade barrier "in a format older binaries already honour". Checking af10e34 showed that no such barrier exists: `store::save`'s refusal fires after the swap and after undo's SavedVariables restore (§2.9). Promising one would be false. What M3 can do is make itself, and every later binary, refuse up front, and say precisely what remains.
  - The widget makes mixed binaries more likely than before (it stamps one binary path), which is why this lands in M3 and not with M4's contract freeze.
- **Rejected:**
  - (i) Bumping the target record version as an M2 barrier: M2 would still write folders and SavedVariables before failing, then leave a stuck journal.
  - (ii) Making M3 journal lines undecodable to M2 on purpose: M2 would then treat the journal as `Unprepared` and prune it, the very hazard above.
  - (iii) A marker file M2 ignores.
- **Tasks:** A3 (journal and history readers, early refusal), D5 and D14 (they write the new lines), D6 (rule 5), D12 (the af10e34 characterization).

#### M3-D46: destructive previews bind to a precondition token
- **Decision.** A new global flag, `--if-match <TOKEN>`, and a `precondition` key in the `--dry-run` data of the five commands it applies to: `remove`, `undo`, `backup restore`, `backup prune` and `errors dismiss`. Elsewhere `--if-match` is a usage error naming those five.
  - **The token** is `pc1:` plus four 16-hex-digit fields: the first 64 bits of a SHA-256 of each canonical part, namely the command path, `targets` (`[{key, generation}…]`), `selection` and `observed`. Keys are sorted, arrays sorted where order carries no meaning. Separate fields let a refusal say which part changed without any stored state. It is computed by one function, `app::precondition`, from the **same plan** the command executes:

    | Command | `selection` | `observed` |
    |---|---|---|
    | `remove` | addon names and the exact folders to delete, per target | nothing beyond `targets` (the record generation covers the selection's inputs) |
    | `undo` | the exact tx ids reverted; the folder plan; the SavedVariables files it would restore | the conflict verdict; for an undo of a whole restore, the live `WTF/` stamp digest (D6) |
    | `backup restore` | backup id, mode, resolved folders and files | the source backup's `backup.json` digest; the live `WTF/` stamp digest (whole) or the candidate files' stamps (`--addon`). The generation is in `targets` |
    | `backup prune` | the exact backup ids it would delete, per target | each victim's `backup.json` digest |
    | `errors dismiss` | each database key it would acknowledge | each database file's stamp and session. Its `targets` part holds target keys **without** generations, because an addon update between reading and dismissing does not change what was shown. `--if-match` requires exactly the token's target set; the widget dismisses one target per call |

  - **Applying.** With `--if-match`, the real run computes the token from its own plan, before staging anything. A different token fails with `plan_stale`, **not retryable** (`PlanStaleSource::Apply`, which exists, `src/error.rs:494-555`). Retrying the same argv with the same token could only fail again, and README's rule that a retryable `plan_stale` reruns its own `fix_argv` would loop.
    - `details.changed` names the parts that differ, from the fixed set `command`, `targets`, `selection` and `observed`.
    - `fix_argv` is the same command with `--dry-run` in place of `--if-match <token>`: preview again. Nothing is changed.
    - Under the lock, the engine's existing generation check then compares against the plan's generations, which equal the token's, so a commit that sneaks in between plan and lock is caught too. With `--if-match`, that refusal is not retryable either.
    - Without `--if-match`, every command behaves as today: the token is an opt-in for previews, never a new requirement for typed commands.
  - **Where tokens come from.** Every `--dry-run` of the five commands. `errors` (the read) also returns `targets[].dismiss.precondition` for the observation it shows, so dismissing what you just looked at needs no extra dry run.
  - **Stateless.** Nothing is stored; a token is valid for exactly as long as the world it describes is unchanged. M4's `plan_id` can embed it.
- **Why.** M3-D9 explains the race, which is a concurrent change between preview and confirm, not a new release. The token is the smallest contract that makes a confirm dialog mean what it says, for the widget and for agents alike. It reuses the existing `plan_stale` code and the engine's generation check.
  - Generations alone are not enough for restores and dismissals: the game and other tools change `WTF/` and BugGrabber files without touching any generation, so the token also covers the files the preview observed.
- **Rejected:** stored plans in M3 (M3-D9); a per-command `--expect-*` flag set; a time-limited token (staleness is about state, not time).
- **Departure.** It brings part of vision §5.11's "plan, then apply" forward from M4. G2 records it.
- **Tasks:** A4 (flag, function, `remove` and `undo`), D4 (`backup prune`), D8 (`backup restore`), B8 (`errors dismiss`), F2 (runner).

#### M3-D47: backup integrity is explicit; `backup verify`
- **Decision.** A backup's `integrity` says what has actually been established about its content, separately from whether it is structurally restorable:
  - `metadata_only`: paths, kinds and sizes were checked against the manifest. **Same-size corruption is not detected**, and output never implies otherwise;
  - `verified`: every file was hashed against manifest hashes that exist. `baseline` records when those hashes were established: `capture` (`backup create --verify`), `import` (checked on import) or `later` (the first `backup verify` of a backup that had none). A `later` baseline proves the content has not changed since then, **not** that it equals what was captured, and the output says exactly that;
  - `damaged`: a check failed. The listing shows why, and a restore refuses with `state_corrupt`.

  The old `restorable` boolean stays in `backup list` (DEC-4), now defined as "structurally restorable and not damaged".
  - **`backup verify <ID>… [-t T]`** hashes each backup's files under a reader reservation (M3-D48).
    - It compares them with the manifest's hashes when present. When absent, it **records** them as a `later` baseline and says "no hashes existed; recorded a baseline (this cannot prove the capture was intact)".
    - It updates `integrity`, `verified_at` and the manifest atomically, rings the doorbell, and appends no history line (a check, not a change of settings). `--dry-run` hashes and reports without recording.
    - Results go per backup, so a damaged backup makes the run `partial`, with exit 0 and `partial: true`.
    - It runs without the global lock.
  - **`backup create --verify`** hashes the staged copy after the clone, outside the lock and before publication, and stores the hashes in the manifest (`baseline: capture`). About 0.5–1 s per 500 MB, so it is opt-in.
  - **Restore verifies when it can.** A restore whose source manifest has hashes checks the staged files against them, outside the lock (M3-D24 step 4). Otherwise it reports `integrity: metadata_only` in its data, never claiming more.
  - **Listing is cheap.** `backup list` reads `backup.json` and the manifest's presence, and never walks or hashes trees. Integrity is what was last recorded, with its time.
- **Why.** The first draft's `restorable: true` meant "paths, kinds and sizes match", and export hashed whatever bytes were there at export time. Neither established that the bytes were the ones captured (review finding). A label that overstates evidence is worse than no label. Verification is opt-in where it costs time, and automatic where hashes already exist.
- **Rejected:** hashing every automatic capture (it breaks the 1 s budget for large trees, and it is the common path); claiming "verified" from a first verification.
- **Tasks:** D1 (model fields), D2 (`--verify`), D8 (restore check), D9 (export check), D10 (import baseline), D13 (`backup verify`).

#### M3-D48: storage pressure, a per-target backup lock and reader reservations
- **Decision.**
  - **Free-space guard.** Before any automatic capture, `statvfs` of `<meta>`'s filesystem must report at least `limits.backup_min_free_mb` (default 2,048 MiB; 0 disables) free for unprivileged users.
    - Below that, retention first runs a **reclamation pass**: it deletes eligible automatic backups, oldest first, never any protected by M3-D32 (the newest qualifying capture, the last 24 h, manual, imported, recovered), and rechecks free space after each deletion.
    - Still below the threshold, the capture is skipped with the warning `backup_space_low` (quiet on change commands; shown by `status` and `backup create --auto`). That includes the case where only protected backups remain.
    - Manual `backup create` warns when below the threshold but proceeds: the user asked.
    - A reflinked backup initially shares data, but the game's later rewrites allocate new space (§2.4 item 8). Filling the filesystem where the game must save its settings is a material failure, which free space, and not apparent size, measures.
  - **Byte-copy budget.** In `daily-copy` mode, apparent bytes are real bytes. The automatic backups of a target are kept within `limits.backup_copy_max_mb` (default 4,096 MiB of apparent size, 0 disables) by pruning eligible ones oldest first. There is no apparent-byte budget for reflinked backups, because apparent bytes would grossly overstate what they use.
  - **Accounting is honest.** Sizes are apparent bytes, labelled as such. `status` and `backup list` show the filesystem's free space next to them, and `WTF.previous` undo snapshots are reported in the same settings total (`snapshot_bytes`).
    - `WTF.previous` follows transaction retention (at most 7 days, M3-D26) and is never reclaimed under pressure: it is undo data, and the only-copy protections of M3-D24 (d) take precedence over space reclamation.
    - It stays outside `SNAPSHOT_MAX_BYTES`, so large restores never evict AddOns undo snapshots (§2.4 item 13).
  - **Per-target scheduling lock.** The automatic due check, capture and publication hold an exclusive, non-blocking `flock` on the target's `<meta>/backups/` directory (`fsx::lock::DirLock::try_exclusive`). A second automatic attempt that finds it held skips as `in_progress`. Manual creates do not take it: two explicit backups at once are two backups.
  - **Reader reservations.** A restore (from plan to commit), an export (the whole stream) and a verify hold a shared `flock` on the backup's own directory (`DirLock::shared`).
    - After locking, the reader re-checks that the path still names the same inode, and a moved or deleted backup is `not_found`.
    - Prune and retention take `DirLock::try_exclusive` on each victim before moving it to trash. A held one is skipped and reported `busy`.
    - The kernel releases `flock`s when a process dies, so a crashed reader never pins a backup.
    - No lock files are created: directories are locked directly.
  - **Lock order.** Backup directory locks are taken before the global lock and never waited on while holding it. Prune's per-victim `try_exclusive` never blocks, and the global lock is held only for its trash renames, as today.
- **Why.** A count limit is not a disk bound. Manual, imported and recovered backups are deliberately unlimited, and `WTF.previous` sits outside the existing snapshot budget (review finding). Two commands deciding "due" at once made duplicate backups, and a concurrent prune could delete a restore's or an export's source mid-read. Safe failure was already guaranteed. Reservations make these common cases simply work, without holding the global lock through long copies.
- **Rejected:** an apparent-byte budget for reflinked backups (it measures the wrong thing); deleting protected backups under pressure; lock files under `<cache>` (a cache wipe would silently break exclusion).
- **Tasks:** D1 (`DirLock`), D3 (guard, budget, scheduling lock), D4 (reclamation, busy), D8, D9 and D13 (reservations).

**Delivery (§11): why the edges are where they are, critical paths and waves, six parallel lanes, collision hot spots, epics and delivery slices (M3 plan, 2026-10-21).** The key → task table (§11.1) is the key → id comment.

Section labels (`§x.y`) and plan keys (A1 … G3) are resolved by the milestone epic body ("How to read the M3 beads") and the key → id comment. Code references are as of `af10e34`.

### 11.2 Why the edges are where they are

- **A1 before every ring site.** Ringing is one function. Tasks that write derived or committed state call it, and a test asserts each does. A1 is small and has no blockers, so it does not delay anything.
- **A2 before every `status` addition.** B7, D11 and E4 add fields to structs A2 creates. One task owns the restructure of `status.rs`, and the rest append.
- **A3 before D5 and D6.** The first journal with new fields and line kinds must be read by a reader that fails closed. Landing the readers first means no build in the tree ever prunes a journal it cannot read (M3-D45).
- **A4 before every destructive surface that binds** (B8, D4, D8) **and before F2.** The token function exists once; each command computes its own parts; the widget's runner needs the flag to exist before its confirm flow can use it.
- **A4 before D6** *(added when the beads were filed)*. D6 extends the `observed` part of undo's token, which lives in A4's `app::precondition`, and tests the resulting `plan_stale`. It changes no start time: D6 waits for D5 (t=6) long after A4 can finish (t=2).
- **A5 before every task that prints a WTF path** (B2, B5, D2, D5, D10). There is one redactor, so there is one mapping.
- **B4 and B5 have no parser dependency.** Attribution and location work on strings and paths. Splitting them from B3 lets two agents build the errors pipeline at once.
- **B8 between B6 and B7.** `status` reads the acknowledgement, so the state file must exist before B7 computes `new`.
- **C3 after B6.** C3 changes the hint `errors` emits, so it lands after `errors` exists.
- **D5 is separate from D8, and D14 from D5.** The engine transaction, with its scope, recovery and retention changes, is reviewed and crash-tested on its own (`TxScene`), before a user-facing command depends on it.
  - D5 stops conservatively wherever preservation would be needed, keeping everything, so it is safe alone.
  - D14 turns those stops into the preservation protocol.
  - D8 waits for both, so no user ever runs a restore whose crash recovery cannot yet preserve a played-on tree.
- **D6 in parallel with D14.** Undo of a restore needs D5's transaction, not D14's protocol. The scenes needing both are D12's.
- **D7 after D8.** Partial restore adds a flag to the command D8 creates, and shares `restore.rs` with D5 and D6. Ordering it last among the restore tasks avoids three-way edits of `undo.rs`.
- **E1 after F3.** The embedded asset table can only `include_str!` files that exist. The plugin is valid only once its two entry points exist (F2's service, F3's bar widget). Views added later append to the table, and E1's set-equality test forces it.
- **F2 after A1 and A4; F8 after B6, B7 and D3.** The core service watches the doorbell and passes tokens. The desktop signals that run `errors` and `backup create --auto` wait for those commands, because templates land with their commands (M3-D2), and for `status`'s errors block, which their triggers read.
- **F6 after B7, B8, C3; F9 after D7, D8, D11.** Each of their views renders a block, or runs a command, that one of those tasks produces.
- **F1 after A2.** The model reducers are written against the triage keys.

### 11.3 Critical path and waves

These are earliest start times with unlimited agents.

```text
t=0  A1 A2 A3 A4 A5 B1 B4 C1 D1 F0
t=1  B2                              (after A5)
t=2  B3 B5 C2                        (after B1+B2; A5+B2; C1)
t=3  D2 D4 D5 D9 D11 F1              (after D1 with A1/A3/A4/A5; F0+A2)
t=4  B6                              (after B3+B4+B5+A1)
t=5  D3 D10 D13 F2                   (after D2+D4; D9; D2; F1+A1+A4)
t=6  B8 C3 D6 D14                    (after B6+A4; B6+C2; D5)
t=8  B7 F3                           (after B8; F2, an L)
t=9  D8                              (after D14, an L, and D6)
t=10 E1 F4 F8                        (after F3; F2+B6+B7+D3)
t=11 D7                              (after D8)
t=12 E2 E4 F5 F6                     (after E1; F4 + B7/B8/C3)
t=13 D12 F9                          (after D7; D7+D8+D11+F4)
t=14 E3                              (after E2)
t=15 F7                              (after F9, the last view)
t=16 G1
t=17 G2
t=18 G3 → done at t=20
```

- **Two critical paths, 20 units each:**
  - the widget and its installer: A2 → F1 → F2 → F3 → E1 → E2 → E3 → G1 → G2 → G3;
  - restore safety: D1 → D5 → D14 → D8 → D7 → F9 → F7 → G1 → G2 → G3.
- **Near-critical (slack 1):** A1, A3, D6, D12, F4, F5, F6.
- **Slack:** the errors lane has 3 units, the WowAce lane 5 to 7, export and import 7, verification 7.
- **What the numbers are, and are not.** Unit arithmetic is **sequencing guidance, not a delivery estimate.**
  - The restore path is the protocol itself: D5's recovery rules, D14's preservation intents and their crash matrices. The third review showed these are new state transitions, not small extensions, and that is where schedule risk lives.
  - Treat A3, A4, B8, C2, D5 and D14 as design gates: each closes only when its adversarial tests pass (common rule 14). Expect them to take longer than their letter.
- **To shorten the path:**
  - staff F2 (an L on the widget path) with the strongest QML agent, and D5/D14 with the engine specialist;
  - start E1's validator and renderer against a fixture plugin tree while F2/F3 run. Only E1's asset table needs F3's files, so E1 can land in two commits.

### 11.4 Six parallel lanes

A simulated assignment with these six lanes, each task starting when its blockers are closed and its lane is free, finishes at t=20, the critical-path length. With five agents the best simulated schedule finishes at t=23, and with four at t=27.

| Agent | Lane | Order (start–end) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Widget | F0 (0–1) → C1 (1–3) → F1 (3–5) → F2 (5–8) → F3 (8–10) → F4 (10–12) → F5 (12–14) → F7 (15–16) | Needs the desktop session for F0 and the F-task real-machine checks. C1 fills the gap while A2 lands |
| 2 | Contract, sources and packaging | A2 (0–3) → A4 (3–5) → C2 (5–7) → C3 (8–10) → E1 (10–12) → E2 (12–14) → E3 (14–16) → G1 (16–17) → G2 (17–18) → G3 (18–20) | A2 first, because F1 and three other tasks wait on it. A4 next, because F2 needs it at t=5 |
| 3 | Errors | A1 (0–2) → B1 (2–4) → B3 (4–6) → B6 (6–8) → B8 (8–10) → B7 (10–12) → F6 (12–14) → E4 (14–15) | A1 first, because D2, D4, D5 and F2 wait on it |
| 4 | Errors inputs, then backup surface | A5 (0–1) → B2 (1–2) → B5 (2–4) → B4 (4–6) → D4 (6–8) → D3 (8–11) → D11 (11–13) → F8 (13–15) | A5 first, because four lanes need the redactor |
| 5 | Restore engine | D1 (0–3) → D5 (3–6) → D14 (6–9) → D8 (9–11) → D7 (11–13) → F9 (13–15) | The engine specialist; owns `journal.rs`, `restore.rs`, `preserve.rs` |
| 6 | Formats, archives and integrity | A3 (0–2) → D2 (3–5) → D9 (5–7) → D6 (7–9) → D10 (9–11) → D13 (11–13) → D12 (13–15) | A3 first, because D5 needs it at t=3. D6 sits here because lane 5 is busy with D14 |

`br ready` decides the real order. The lanes are a starting assignment that keeps collision hot spots inside one lane where possible.

**Collision hot spots** (coordinate through `SendMessage` and claim comments listing files):

| File | Tasks | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `src/app/status.rs` | A2, B7, D11, E4 | A2 lands first; the others append fields and recommendations |
| `src/app/undo.rs`, `src/engine/undo.rs` | A2, A3, A4, D3, D6, D7 | A2's `select` refactor first; A3's rule 5 and A4's token are separate functions; lane 6 owns D6, lane 5 owns D7 |
| `src/engine/tx.rs` | A1, A3, D3, D5 | A1's ring is one line; A3's early refusal is one call before staging; D3's hook sits before `stage_all`; D5 adds failpoints. Rebase carefully |
| `src/engine/journal.rs` | A1, A3, D5, D14 | A3 first (readers), then D5 (writer selection, waits, conservative stop), then D14 (preservation) |
| `src/fsx/scope.rs` | D5, D9, E2 | Each adds a row or case with its own scope test |
| `src/fsx/sys.rs`, `mutate.rs`, `lock.rs` | D1, D5, D9 | D1 adds `ClonePolicy`, `StampDigest`, `DirLock`; D5 the exchange probe; D9 the directory fsync after persist |
| `src/fsx/prune.rs`, `tests/single_writer.rs` | D2, D4, D10, E2, E3 | Each adds its `Kind`/`PRUNE_CALLERS` entry; D4 adds the read-only-dir fix |
| `src/error.rs` | B6, B8, D2, D3, D5, D8, D9, E2, E4 | Additive macro rows plus count bumps: merge conflicts are trivial, and the counts must be right |
| `src/cli.rs`, `src/app/mod.rs`, help tests | A4, B6, B8, D1, D2, D4, D8, D9, D10, D13, E2, E3 | One `Command` variant per top-level command (`errors`, `backup`, `omarchy`); subcommand variants added in their tasks; A4's global flag first |
| `src/limits.rs` + snapshot | A2, A5, B1, B3, B5, B6, C2, D1, D2, D3, D4, D10, D11, E2, E3 | Re-accept the snapshot in each task; §7.11 names each constant's task |
| `tests/engine_crash.rs` | D3, D5, D6, D7, D14, D12 | Each task adds its own shape and matrix; D12 adds cross-feature scenes |
| `omarchy/Service.qml` | F2, F8 | F2 first; F8 adds signal handlers and templates only |
| `README.md` | everyone | Each task edits only its own section; G1 reconciles |
| `Cargo.toml` | D9 | The only crate additions in M3 |

### 11.5 Epics

| Epic | Children | Delivers |
|---|---|---|
| M3 milestone epic | the 7 area epics | §3.3 criteria |
| A: contract foundations | A1–A5 | Doorbell; triage blocks; fail-closed formats; preview tokens; the privacy redactor |
| B: Lua errors | B1–B8 | `errors`; `errors dismiss`; status errors |
| C: keyless BugGrabber | C1–C3 | `wowace:` source; catalog variants |
| D: backups and restore | D1–D14 | `backup` command tree; restore transactions; preservation; verification |
| E: widget packaging | E1–E4 | `omarchy` command tree; widget in `status` |
| F: the widget | F0–F9 | The Omarchy plugin |
| G: docs and checkpoint | G1–G3 | README, vision, checkpoint |

### 11.6 Delivery slices

The lanes run in parallel, but progress is judged by **four slices**, each with a demonstrable exit. When a slice's last task closes, the agent closing it runs the slice's demo and records it as a comment on the milestone epic, in the `[x] … : evidence` style. A slice whose demo fails reopens the task responsible (`--deps discovered-from`). Nothing waits for G3 to discover that two halves do not fit.

| Slice | Tasks | Exit demo | §3.3 items it pre-checks |
|---|---|---|---|
| **S1. See and update from the bar** | A1, A2, A4, F0, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, E1, E2, E3, E4 | `omarchy install` on the desktop; the badge follows a terminal `update` within 1 s; update one addon from the panel, undo it; a `remove` preview gone stale gives `plan_stale`; reinstall swaps atomically | 1, 2 (the terminal-change part), 3, 4 (update states), 5, 13 (`remove`, `undo`) |
| **S2. Capture and diagnose** | A5, B1–B8, C1–C3, D1–D4, D11, D13, F6, F8 | `errors` on every client, read-only; `install buggrabber` keyless on retail and wotlk; automatic checkpoints before a change and after a simulated session, coalesced; `backup verify`; the Issues view with strict output, received reports and a bound dismissal | 6, 7, 8 (create, auto, verify), 13 (`errors dismiss`, `backup prune`) |
| **S3. Recover** | A3, D5, D6, D14, D8, D7, F9 | whole and `--addon` restores from the CLI and from the bar's chooser, each undone; the crash matrices of D5, D6, D7 and D14 | 8 (restore), 9, 13 (`backup restore`), 14 |
| **S4. Portability and close** | D9, D10, D12, F7, G1, G2, G3 | export → import → restore byte-identical; integration scenes; the af10e34 characterization; perf; gate from a clean checkout; README | 8 (export, import), 9 (integration), 10, 11, 12, 14 (the characterization) |
